title: feat(vta): discharge the backup family's spec debt, and audit what it was hiding
body:
trust-tasks-rs 0.17.7 carries the six specs from trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#347, so `vta/backup/*` and `vta/management/reload-services` come off `UNSPECCED_DISPATCHED_URIS` and gain conformance witnesses.

The reduction plan's §D suggestion of a top-level `backup/*` was **not** taken: the family is agent lifecycle, and `vta/` is where the rest of it lives.

That was meant to be bookkeeping. It was not.

## Making them visible showed three of them succeeding silently

The audit census could not see these tasks before — an unspecced task has no witness, and an undriven task reports nothing. The moment it could, it found three consequential successes leaving **no trace at all**:

| task | what it does | trail |
|---|---|---|
| `initiate-export` | mints a **fetchable copy of the entire agent** at a known address | none |
| `initiate-import` | opens a **writable endpoint into** the agent | none |
| `reload-services` | restarts the agent, dropping every open session | none |

None of the three alters stored state, which is why nothing state-shaped ever caught them: the only evidence these operations happened is the row that was not being written.

`reload-services` is the sharper case. It *had* an audit call — the `audit!` macro, which emits a `tracing` event and never touches the `AuditSink`, so nothing it recorded reached `audit/list` or an operator's external sink. That is precisely the defect the census module header describes, sitting undetected in a task the census could not drive. Its sink write goes **before** `trigger_restart`, because the restart tears down the runtime the write is running in.

## Three more the census structurally cannot reach

`complete-export`, `finalize-import` and `abort` were silent on success too, and the sweep would never have said so: all three need a real bundle, the census drives an empty store, and it therefore only ever sees their not-found refusals. **It would have reported this family green.**

Found by reading rather than by the sweep, and the blind spot is now written into the helper's doc comment — a test that cannot reach a path cannot vouch for it, and a green census must not be mistaken for coverage of these three.

`finalize-import` matters most. On commit it replaces the agent's keys, ACLs, contexts **and its audit trail**, so a row written into imported state would document its own erasure. It is recorded to the sink after the op returns, which is outside the state the import replaced — the same reasoning the specification gives for the response being the record the *operator* holds.

## Witnesses

Both `password` fixtures carry an obvious non-secret, and so does `transportToken`. The specification's schema directory deliberately holds no specimen password — a fixture value is the one thing implementers copy — and a witness is read far more often than a spec.

`finalize-import`'s request pins `confirm: false`. A committing witness would be the one shape in that table whose meaning is "replace the agent", and a fixture is the wrong place to spell that.

`reload-services` pins the empty object, which is what conforms: every member that task might carry would be a way of asking the agent to run on something other than its configuration.

## Verification

- `cargo test -p vta-service` — 1014 lib tests and all 25 integration binaries, green.
- `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy -p vta-service --all-features`, `cargo check --workspace` — clean. (`--workspace`, not `--all-targets`, which masked a cfg-gating bug in #1235.)

Stacked on #1238, now merged; rebased onto main.

title: ci: add checks and a release path
body:
This repository had no `.github` directory. Two releases' worth of a credential library — including `authority::verify_chain`, which is the part that decides whether a holder acquired authority they were never granted — merged on local runs alone, and every version on crates.io got there by someone running `cargo publish` from a laptop.

That is not a hypothetical cost. **0.6.0 has been merged and unreleased since the day it landed**, because nothing turns a merge into a published crate. The data-rooms work in `verifiable-trust-infrastructure` needs `authority::verify_chain` and cannot compile against it; that workspace deliberately has no `[patch.crates-io]`, and `vti-rooms` publishes, so a git dependency is not an option either. This is the actual gate on that track.

## What this adds

**`ci.yml`** — fmt, clippy (`-D warnings`), tests, MSRV (1.95.0), and `cargo package --locked`. The last one because a crate that cannot be packaged cannot be released, and finding that out at tag time means the tag is already wrong.

**`publish.yml`** — publishes on a `vX.Y.Z` tag push.

- The trigger is the **tag push**, not `release: published`: a Release created with the default `GITHUB_TOKEN` does not cascade-trigger other workflows, so that handler would silently never fire.
- Auth is **crates.io Trusted Publishing** (OIDC), so no long-lived token lives in this repo. It needs one manual step, written into the workflow header — on crates.io, under the crate's *Settings → Trusted Publishing*, add owner `OpenVTC`, repository `dtg-credentials`, workflow `publish.yml`. Until that exists the job fails at the auth step naming exactly this.
- It checks the tag against `Cargo.toml` before doing anything. The two disagree exactly once — when someone tags before the version bump lands — and the result is a release number that means nothing.
- It skips a version already on crates.io, so a tag re-pushed after a failed run recovers instead of dying on `crate version already uploaded`, which would otherwise force a version bump nothing needed.

## What CI found on its first run

The `--no-default-features` job failed. Both examples call `.sign()`, which lives behind `affinidi-signing`, so a consumer who disables default features got a missing-method error naming the method rather than the disabled backend. They now declare `required-features`. The library and its tests were always fine — 53 of the 58 tests run without the signing backend.

## Releasing 0.6.0 after this merges

1. Configure Trusted Publishing on crates.io (once, as above).
2. `git tag v0.6.0 && git push origin v0.6.0`.

`Cargo.toml` already reads `0.6.0` and the changelog section is already written, so nothing else is needed.

title: fix(vta): audit every refusal, and make the census that missed them measure
body:
#1236 shipped a census reporting **72 consequential tasks that "audit on success only"**, with a budget and a note that fixing them would be ~60 handlers in one diff. The number was right and everything else was wrong.

## The census was measuring one gate, 72 times

It built each document with `TrustTask::new(id, type_uri, payload)`. That envelope carries no `issuer`, `recipient`, `issuedAt` or `proof`, and the spine enforces all four *before* dispatch — so all 72 documents were refused `422 expired` at the freshness check and **not one handler ever ran**.

One unaudited code path, exercised once per task, reported as a per-handler finding. The `silent_on_success` invariant beside it passed **vacuously** for the same reason: nothing ever succeeded, so nothing could succeed silently.

A census whose fixtures cannot get past the front door reports the door, once per caller, and looks like a survey.

## What the gate was hiding — the real defect

`dispatch_trust_task_validated` has a dozen early returns (expiry, wrong recipient, replay, schema validation, proof failure, the policy gate). The blanket vault audit sat a few lines above that function's final `return`, so it recorded the outcomes that reached the bottom and none that did not.

Its own doc-comment claimed *"read or write, success or denied — produces exactly one persisted audit row"*. That was true only of denials the **handler** raised. A document refused at the envelope gate left no trace at all, for any task in any family.

That is the refusal an incident review most wants: not "the handler said no", but *"something arrived claiming to be this, signed like this, and never got that far"*.

## The fix is one frame, not sixty handlers

`DispatchAudit` is captured in `dispatch_trust_task_inner` and recorded around the call to `dispatch_trust_task_validated`. No early return inside can bypass it, and a fourteenth added tomorrow inherits it.

Two dispositions, to avoid doubling the trail:

| | recorded |
|---|---|
| vault family | every outcome — **behaviour unchanged** |
| everything else consequential | **refusals only** — successes are the handler's row |

Non-vault refusals record as `task.refused` with the URI as the resource, not under the operation's name. The handler vocabulary does not follow the URI (`acl/grant/0.1` → `acl.create`, `keys/create/0.1` → `key.create`, `auth/revoke-session/0.1` → `session.revoke`), so matching it needs an 84-entry table that goes stale invisibly — and it would file a lie, since these refusals happen before dispatch: no ACL was consulted, no key was touched.

**Overlap is exactly one task.** `task-consent/decision/0.1` audits its own refusal and now gets a second row. The other ten already-audited refusals are vault-family and take the unchanged branch.

## The census now measures what it claims

Conforming envelopes — issued now, addressed to this agent, issued by the DID the claims authenticate, signed — so documents reach handlers.

- **`silent_on_failure`: 50 → 0.** 50 is what the number actually was once the gate stopped swallowing the run. The budget is replaced by a hard invariant; a gap closed structurally does not need a ratchet.
- **`silent_on_success`: 2, neither a defect.** `auth/revoke-session` and `consent/revoke` take documented no-op arms against the census's empty store — *"a revoke that deleted nothing is not a state change worth a line"*. New `NO_AUDIT_WHEN_NO_OP` list rather than `NO_AUDIT_BY_DESIGN`, because that list claims no trail is *ever* correct and these audit fine when they change something. Conflating them would license "fixing" a handler into recording work it did not do.
- **New assertion: at least five tasks must actually succeed.** A sweep where nothing does is measuring the gate again — this is the check that would have caught the original.

## Verification

- Census **proved non-vacuous**: disabling the refusal branch fails it with exactly the 50 it closes.
- `cargo test -p vta-service` — 1014 lib tests plus every integration binary, all green.
- `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy -p vta-service --all-features`, `cargo check --workspace` (not `--all-targets`, which masked a cfg-gating bug in #1235) — clean.

title: feat(rooms): rooms end to end — storage, dispatch, client, DID templates, MLS
body:
**Track 2.2** of the data-rooms delivery plan, complete: storage, authorization and
Trust-Task dispatch for `rooms/{create,records/{put,get,list},epoch/mint}`.

## A correction: this was not blocked

I initially split this PR because I thought dispatch needed the `rooms/*` schemas published.
**It doesn't**, and I checked rather than kept asserting it:

- The schema gate is a `#[cfg(test)]` conformance sweep scoped to `spec/vtc/` — this family
  is top-level `spec/rooms/`, so the sweep does not cover it.
- `parse_payload` is generic over any `DeserializeOwned`. No generated type is required.

So the wire types are hand-written in `rooms::wire` against the schemas in
[dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#346](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/346) —
the same shape `vta_sdk::protocols` already uses for the VTA's families. **When those
bindings publish, replace them rather than keeping both**: two definitions of one wire
format is how casing drift gets in, and this workspace has paid for that.

## The invariant, and how it is defended

`rooms::authz` reads **no ACL, no roster, no session**. A room operation is authorized by
the authority chain the room itself issued, which is what makes a room portable — the moment
host state participates in a room decision, the room cannot move and this service has joined
its membership.

Two structural defences, because this is the easiest invariant in the design to lose by
accident:

- **Handlers take no `AuthClaims`.** Its absence is the point, not an omission.
- **`AuthorizedAction` is constructible only by `authorize()`** — the workspace's typestate
  discipline, so a handler cannot skip the check or substitute its own.

## What it deliberately refuses

**The sealed tiers, for now.** Cryptographic chain verification needs the room's DID
resolved to a verification method, which arrives with `attributed`. Until then, serving a
sealed room would mean serving one whose chain nobody checked — so it refuses, loudly, with
a test pinning the refusal so it cannot be relaxed by accident.

The **private-tier subject binding** is enforced already, even though the tier is refused,
because it is a schema-level property: without it two parties pool credentials — one
contributes membership, the other authority — and the combination verifies as a single party
holding both.

## Storage invariants, each with a test

An `open` room refuses ciphertext and a sealed room refuses cleartext · a `private` room
refuses a recorded author · a record sealed under a stale epoch is refused · an epoch
advances by exactly one · versions are monotonic **per room** · a conflict **carries the
current version** so a caller need not re-read · a watermark listing returns **tombstones**,
without which deletions never propagate · retract and purge are separate verbs · the record
prefix is room-exact, so room `a` never returns room `ab`'s records.

## Notes for review

- `ROOMS` / `ROOM_RECORDS` are in `ALL` **and** `BACKED_UP` (they must partition `ALL`
  exactly). The census moves to 27, and I added the matching `AppState` fields and opened the
  keyspaces — the census test's own doc says `ALL` must track those fields, so satisfying the
  length check alone would have left the documented invariant false.
- The dispatcher census test lists the rooms URIs with a note that they name **hand-written
  constants rather than generated `TYPE_URI`s**, so the property it guarantees is weaker for
  them until #346 publishes. Stated in the test rather than left for a reader to infer.

25 tests across the three layers. `cargo test -p vtc-service`: **950 lib + 104 integration
passing**, clippy clean.

## 🤖 New release * `vta-sdk`: 0.32.3 -> 0.32.4 (✓ API compatible changes) * `vti-common`: 0.16.1 -> 0.16.2 (✓ API compatible changes) * `vta-cli-common`: 0.12.3 -> 0.12.4 (✓ API compatible changes) * `cnm-cli`: 0.13.3 -> 0.13.4 * `pnm-cli`: 0.14.3 -> 0.14.4 * `vta-service`: 0.23.4 -> 0.23.5 (✓ API compatible changes)
Changelog

## `vta-sdk`

## [0.32.4](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/compare/vta-sdk-v0.32.3...vta-sdk-v0.32.4) — 2026-09-02 ### Added - **vta**: Implement vta/credentials/list, and check the vault/credentials family ([#1235](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1235)) * feat(vta): implement vta/credentials/list, and check the vault/credentials family `vta/credentials` served `issue` and `revoke` and nothing else, so an issuer could not ask its own agent what it had issued. The `credentialId` that `revoke` is keyed on is returned exactly once, in the `issue` response; a caller that did not record it at that moment could not recover it at all. Specified upstream as `vta/credentials/list/0.1` (trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#342). This implements it — a read over records that already exist. `IssuedCredentialRecord` carries the id, holder, both instants and the revocation instant and reason, and revocation is a tombstone rather than a delete, so a revoked credential is still there to list. No new storage. Bodies are never returned. `vault/list/0.1` states the rule this follows — list enumerates, release uses — and `summarise` is the one place the projection happens, so "a summary never carries the credential" is enforced rather than remembered. `status` is derived at read time with `revoked` beating `expired`: reporting a revoked credential as merely expired would hide that somebody acted, and a stored status is wrong one second after it is written. Gated on `require_manage`, not the Admin-plus-step-up its mutating siblings use. An operator who may read the ACL and the policy set may read what their own agent issued — same category of question — and a step-up that fires on every page of a list is one people learn to clear without reading. The read is audited anyway: "who enumerated the issuance log" is what an incident review asks, and nothing else would record it.
## `vti-common`
## [0.16.2](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/compare/vti-common-v0.16.1...vti-common-v0.16.2) — 2026-09-02 ### Added - **acl**: Add MemoryRead/MemoryWrite and gate the memory tasks on them ([#1234](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1234)) There was no read-only grant on agent memory. The gate in trust_tasks/memory.rs was auth.require_context and nothing else, and a context is binary: any DID that could reach one could also write and delete every memory in it. So an operator could not give an agent read-only access to their own memory, and the --read-only flag in vta-mcp's guard is a client-side glob filter that a caller talking to the VTA directly never encounters. The published specification already assumes the split exists. specs/vta/memory/delete/0.1/spec.md reasons about "a VTA whose write capability is granted more freely than its read capability", and about callers holding write without read. There was no read capability and no write capability; there was a context. The ACL supplied nothing finer either - the act axis is (role, allowed_contexts) decoded to a three-valued ActScope, a where with no what. Adds Capability::{MemoryRead, MemoryWrite}, wires them through derived_capabilities_for_role, and gates the three handlers. Legacy rows carry no explicit capability set and fall back to the derived mapping, so the roles that write memory today keep writing it. Deliberate behaviour changes, both tightenings: - reader loses memory write. A read-only consumer of a context should not be able to rewrite the memories in it. - monitor loses memory access entirely. It is the least-privileged role and the Default for AuthClaims, precisely so a fixture that leaks past its expected reach lands somewhere harmless - which it did not, while memory was context-gated alone. application keeps both, deliberately and with a test saying why: vta-agent-memory grants exactly that role so the memory service is not the user, and every existing install would otherwise stop saving. The capability is checked before the context, so a caller missing it cannot use the reason text to probe which contexts exist. Note the canonical Capability enum in the trust-tasks registry (device/_shared/0.1) is already behind this crate - it carries neither sign-trust-task nor credential-write. A spec PR reconciling all four follows separately; this change does not widen that gap unilaterally so much as make it worth closing. Implements the orthogonal fix called out in docs/05-design-notes/data-rooms.md 11.1.
## `vta-cli-common`
## [0.12.4](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/compare/vta-cli-common-v0.12.3...vta-cli-common-v0.12.4) — 2026-09-02 ### Fixed - **sdk**: Accept the `ext` member every payload schema declares ([#1231](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1231)) SPEC §4.5.1 gives every Trust Task payload an `ext` slot, and the published schemas declare it — `acl/list/0.1` lists `ext` among its properties, as do `policy/list/0.2`, every `vta/memory/*` body, `app-state` writes, config show and patch, and both credential-issuance bodies. Sixteen `deny_unknown_fields` structs had no field for it, so a producer doing exactly what the schema permits had its whole document rejected: malformed request: payload parse: unknown field `ext`, expected one of `role`, `scope`, `direction`, `subjectPrefix`, `pageSize`, `cursor` Seven sibling structs already carry `ext`, with the reasoning written out on each; this completes that work rather than starting it. `deny_unknown_fields` stays: carrying `ext` explicitly is what keeps a *typo* refused, which is the guard that clause was there for, while letting through the one member the spec says is always allowed. Found from a browser-based VTA management console: its Access and Policy panes died outright, and the operator was shown a parse error naming a field the spec had told the client it could send. Nothing caught it earlier because whether a caller trips this is decided entirely by whether it populates `ext` — the conformance table exercises the members its fixtures set, and this defect lives in the member they leave unset. So the guard is a census over the source rather than another fixture: `payload_ext_census.rs` fails on any `deny_unknown_fields` type under `protocols/` that carries no `ext`, with an exceptions list that has to state a reason. Verified to fail by reverting one struct.

title: WD02 merge plan: sequencing the five outstanding PRs into a consistent whole
body:
Per [#22](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/22#issuecomment-5465297803), @stormer78 and I have the ball on assembling WD02. Five of the six open PRs can merge into a consistent document; this issue records the sequence, the per-PR work each needs before merging, and — the reason this needs its own issue — four decisions that belong to no single PR. The goal is that every merge closes the issues it can close, and nothing lands that a later PR has to un-say.

@stormer78's combined preview branch (`stormer78:preview/wd02-combined`) proved that `main` + #30 + #19 + #29 renders as one document, which is most of the confidence we need. But that preview omits #26 and #27, so the full five-PR integration has not yet been assembled by anyone — and the two it omits are the ones with a vocabulary dependency on #30's ordering. Hence the sequence below.

## Proposed merge order

**#26 → #27 → #30 → #19 → #29**

1. **#26 (edge verifiability, closes #21).** First because its new normative section is written in `[[ref: M-DID]]` / `[[ref: R-DID]]` vocabulary. If #30 merges first, those term files are deleted and #26's references dangle, forcing a semantic rewrite; if #26 lands first, #30's document-wide sweep picks the section up as ordinary prose. Needs a rebase onto current `main` first.
2. **#27 (max-of-halves privacy consideration; closes #23 together with #30).** Same vocabulary logic, and it needs the privacy-consideration renumber already flagged on the thread (#20's item 7 landed in its slot; #12 took 8).
3. **#30 (correlation scope, closes #22).** The big sweep. Its rebase re-words #26's section and shortens #27's paragraph to the one-line rule — both PR descriptions already anticipate exactly this. Housekeeping: the body says "Implements #22," which is not an auto-close keyword; add "Closes #22."
4. **#19 (VDC).** Rebased over #30's vocabulary and current `main`, review feedback folded in, undrafted. Checklist below.
5. **#29 (VAC).** Last, because it depends on the vocabulary and on the VDC existing for its cross-references. Checklist below.

**#18 stays out, deliberately.** It is parked as draft pending the vti-spec repo, per @bmiller59's plan to split it between cred-spec content and cross-cutting material. It is blocked on an external event, not on this merge — so it is not a gap in WD02. #11 stays open with it; #17 mostly resolves inside this merge (see D-A).

## Pre-merge work per PR

**#19 (VDC):**

- Rebase over #30: R-DID/M-DID/C-DID/P-DID vocabulary throughout the diff becomes declared-scope language.
- Privacy item 7 currently recommends issuing VDCs "against an R-DID rather than an M-DID." Under three scopes the honest value is **`directed`, not `pairwise`**: a VDC is presented to arbitrary verifiers, each of whom sees the delegator's identifier, so it is known to a holder-chosen set by construction. #30 makes exactly this argument for the witness identifier ("`directed` at minimum"); the delegator's identifier follows the same precedent — a context-scoped `directed` identifier per delegation.
- Fold in the review feedback from @sankarshanmukhopadhyay and @bmiller59: acceptance unconditionally required, fail-closed `maxDepth` confirmed, delegate eligibility per VTC governance, VDC scoped to delegation only (guardianship/succession excluded).
- The digest-encoding change stays in this PR and becomes the vehicle for the settled `digestMultibase` decision — see D-A. On rebase it must widen to cover **both** digest members now on `main` (#12 added the member-issued VMC acknowledgement's `digest` alongside the VWC's), and carry #12's canonicalization clause (top-level `proof` excluded from the hashed representation), which the current diff predates.
- Undraft once the above are pushed.

**#29 (VAC):**

- Drop the `community_did.md` edit. The sequencing comment already concluded the C-DID amendment "has nothing left to amend," but the diff still modifies the file #30 deletes — an edit-vs-delete conflict waiting for whoever merges second.
- The node-type editor's note ("the four VID types cover neither service nodes...") is written against the taxonomy #30 retires. Under declared scope the answer is trivially "a DID with a declared scope," so the note should be deleted rather than rewritten.
- Reconcile the VDC↔VAC cross-references. #19's delegation-vs-authority table says authority is "not defined in this specification" and deliberately leaves the word free; once #29 merges, that row and the "left free" note are false. Neither PR's diff can fix this today (the VDC is not on `main`), so #29's rebase carries it.
- Place the VAC per the outcome of D-B, or carry an editor's note if D-B is still open.

## Decisions that belong to no single PR

**D-A — Digest encoding: settled, `digestMultibase` is the standard.** Recording it here because the agreement was reached among the cred spec editors and is not fully visible in any one thread: WD02 adopts Multibase/Multihash digest values per VC Data Integrity §2.6, replacing `sha256:`+hex. This is consistent with the direction already on the record — #17 items 1–2, the implementation in #18, and the Trust Tasks framework's own adoption of the mechanism as §4.9.3 (trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#236) — so both layers agree on the encoding. What remains is only carriage: with #18 parked, **#19's Digest Encoding section becomes the vehicle**, exactly as @stormer78's preview branch resolved it. On rebase it applies to all three digest-valued members (the VWC `digest`, the member-issued VMC acknowledgement's `digest` from #12, and the VDC's `parent`/`accepts`), preserves #12's exclude-`proof` canonicalization clause, and #17 can then close at #19's merge with a comment noting that item 3 (`DataIntegrityProof` suites) travels with the #18 split.

**D-B — Credential taxonomy after eight types (resolves #28).** No open PR implements #28, and its proposed fix (two categories, VIC standalone) is overtaken by the new credentials. The deciding variable is the question #29 deliberately left open — where the VDC sits:

- **VDC in Edge Credentials** (as #19 proposes, and as the delegation-is-not-authority sections of both PRs argue): Edge = VRC, VMC, VDC; Annotation = VPC, VWC, VEC; VIC and VAC each stand alone — recreating the single-subsection problem #28 exists to fix, twice.
- **VDC in Authority Credentials** next to the VAC: three well-formed categories plus standalone VIC — structurally clean, but it files a delegation credential under a heading both PRs spend real effort distinguishing it from.

The categories are informative, so a third option is open: keep the semantic split (VDC = edge) and fix the outline editorially — promote VIC and VAC to top-level sections named for their credential, per @talltree's rule in #28 that no section should have exactly one subsection. My lean is that third option. Whichever way, it is a WG call to make here, not a side effect of merging.

**D-C — Consideration-list structure.** #27, #30, #19, and #29 all append to the Security and Privacy lists; the preview showed Security reaching fifteen items, and every later PR renumbers again. Proposal: the **last** PR in the sequence (#29) restructures both lists under short subheadings in the same push, so the churn happens once. Volunteers welcome to disagree with the grouping there rather than in five rebases.

**D-D — Disposition of #24.** #26's per-verifier definition answers #24's three questions in principle (different VTNs → the anchor sets the verifier accepts; deliberately unanchored → verifiable as far as those anchors reach; external verifier → the definition's home case), and @mitchuski endorsed that resolution on both threads. But #26 does not say "closes #24," and the answers are implicit. Proposal: when #26 merges, close #24 with a comment stating the three answers explicitly, unless anyone wants them added to the normative text first.

## What this plan closes, and what stays open

| Issue | Disposition |
|---|---|
| #21 | Closed by #26 |
| #22 | Closed by #30 (add the keyword on rebase) |
| #23 | Closed once #27 and #30 are both in |
| #24 | Closed at #26 with an explicit comment (D-D) |
| #28 | Closed by the D-B decision, implemented in #29's rebase or a small follow-up |
| #9 | **Stays open — and gains weight.** After this merge, four things lean on the unencoded common-control linkage: both existing ZKP constructions (the community-anchored one now crossing identifiers by default under #30), the VAC's shared-subject rule, and the VDC's delegation predicate. #26's note marks the dependency honestly; the resolution is cross-TF work with the ZKP task force. |
| #17 | Closed at #19's merge (D-A): items 1–2 land there; item 3 (`DataIntegrityProof` suites) travels with the #18 split, noted in the closing comment |
| #11 | Stays open with parked #18 / the vti-spec split |
| #25 | Stays open — proposes a new discovery mechanism no PR implements; orthogonal to this merge |

If the order and the four decisions look right, #26 can rebase immediately — nothing in it waits on anything above.

title: feat(rooms): add the rooms/keys oracle pair
body:
Follows [#346](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/346) (merged). Two
tasks that let an **AI agent use a data room without holding its principal's keys or
credentials**.

## The distinction this pair exists to make

`rooms/keys/open` decrypts one sealed record and returns the plaintext.
`rooms/keys/present` produces a presentation for one operation.

**Neither returns key material or credentials.** That is the design rather than a detail. An
agent runs on a general-purpose machine, and a key-release call would leave it holding —
indefinitely, on that machine — material belonging to *every other member* of the room.

Two properties follow that key release cannot offer:

- **Revoking the agent actually revokes it.** There is nothing else for it to keep.
- **The blast radius of a compromised agent is bounded by time**, not by the lifetime of a
  key it was handed.

## Details worth reviewing

**`action` is required on `present`, not a hint.** A presentation is scoped to what it was
asked for and cannot be replayed for something else. An implementation that mints one
covering every action has handed the caller its principal's whole standing — the outcome
attenuation exists to prevent.

**An oracle MUST NOT produce a presentation conferring an action the principal does not
hold.** A caller cannot acquire authority by asking for it, and `actionNotHeld` says so
plainly rather than returning something that fails at a verifier for reasons the caller
cannot diagnose.

**`open` refuses rather than guesses.** A record that does not authenticate was sealed under
a different key or has been relocated. Trying keys until one works would turn a detectable
relocation into a silent one.

## The trade, stated rather than glossed

Security & Privacy says it outright: **the oracle sees plaintext**, because it is the
principal's own infrastructure and already in their trusted computing base — which a host is
not, and is why a host sees only ciphertext. And an oracle that cached opened plaintext would
create a second copy of the room outside the room.

## Recipe

- `npm run validate` — **367 specs, no errors and no warnings** (Security & Privacy sections
  and their four sub-headings written, not allowlisted)
- `cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen && cargo fmt --all` — 362 payload modules
- `npm run build-ts-bindings` — 429 TS modules
- `npm run check-bindings` — *367 specifications checked against 367 TypeScript and 362 Rust modules — all agree*
- `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs` — green

**Additive, so a patch bump**: `trust-tasks-rs` 0.17.6 → 0.17.7, `trust-tasks-ts` 0.16.7 →
0.16.8. (Same reasoning as #346 — new families add modules and types; there is no slug enum
for a consumer to match exhaustively, and a leading-component bump would be a seven-crate
workspace event for a change that breaks nobody.)

## Why spec-first

The VTA's dispatcher refuses a URI the published registry has no schema for, and its own
harness says *"serving a NEW unspecced URI fails — add the spec upstream, do not grow this
list."* So the oracle's implementation waits on this, rather than the other way round.

title: ci: add checks and a release path
body:
ci: add checks and a release path

This repository had no .github directory. Two releases' worth of a
credential library merged on local runs alone, and every version on
crates.io got there by someone running cargo publish from a laptop.

That is not hypothetical cost. 0.6.0 - the release carrying the VAC and
VDC - has been merged and unreleased since the day it landed, because
there was no path that turned a merge into a published crate. The
data-rooms work in verifiable-trust-infrastructure needs
authority::verify_chain and cannot compile against it, and the workspace
there deliberately has no [patch.crates-io], so a git dependency is not
an option either. A tag is now the release.

ci.yml runs fmt, clippy (-D warnings), tests, the MSRV check, and
cargo package --locked - the last because a crate that cannot be
packaged cannot be released, and learning that at tag time means the tag
is already wrong.

publish.yml goes on a vX.Y.Z tag push rather than release: published,
because a Release created with the default GITHUB_TOKEN does not
cascade-trigger other workflows and that handler would silently never
fire. Auth is crates.io Trusted Publishing, so no long-lived token lives
here; the one-time crates.io setup is written into the workflow header,
and until it exists the job fails at the auth step naming exactly that.
It checks the tag against Cargo.toml first - the two disagree exactly
once, when someone tags before the bump lands, and the result is a
release number that means nothing - and skips a version already on
crates.io so a re-pushed tag recovers instead of dying on 'already
uploaded'.

The no-default-features job found a real break on its first run: both
examples call .sign(), which lives behind affinidi-signing, so a
consumer disabling default features hit a missing-method error naming
the method rather than the feature. They now declare required-features.
The library and its tests were always fine - 53 of the 58 tests run
without the backend.

title: test(trust-tasks): fix doc() helper ignoring issued_at, cover the unboundable-window case
body:
## What

Fixes a bug in the `freshness_bounds::doc()` test helper: it always seeded a fresh default `issuedAt` regardless of its `issued_at: Option<&str>` argument, so `doc(None, None)` never actually built a document without one, and the test that name implied went unexercised for as long as it existed.

## What this PR does

With the helper fixed to genuinely omit `issuedAt` when `None` is passed, replaces the one test that relied on the broken helper with three that cover the actual behavior:

- a truly timestamp-less document is refused under a bounded `FreshnessPolicy` (`max_age.is_some()`) with `RejectReason::Stale { detail: Unboundable }` — SPEC §7.2 *Bounding the record*: a consumer retaining a bounded window has nowhere to place a document it can't measure the age of.
- `expiresAt` alone is sufficient without `issuedAt`.
- the same timestamp-less document is accepted under a policy with no window at all.

All six `freshness_bounds` tests pass with nothing ignored. `cargo test`, `cargo clippy`, and `cargo fmt --all --check` are clean.

## History

The first version of this PR mischaracterized the wire-level `expired` code on this path as a §7.2 item 13 violation. [@stormer78 corrected this](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1229#issuecomment-5490325599): the `expired` code here is `trust-tasks-rs`'s mapping of an internal `Stale { detail: Unboundable }` reason (there's no narrower standard code for it), governed by §7.2's *Bounding the record* clause, not item 13 — and it's driven by this VTA's own `freshness_policy()` choosing a bounded 10-minute window, not by a defect in the crate. Verified directly against the `trust-tasks-rs` 0.17.3 source (`freshness.rs:216-228`, `error.rs:525`). No upstream report needed.

title: feat(vta): spec the backup family and reload-services
body:
Six families the VTA dispatches today and nothing described: `vta/backup/{initiate-export, complete-export, initiate-import, finalize-import, abort}/1.0` and `vta/management/reload-services/1.0`.

All five backup verbs rather than the one a management console needs. A partial family is worse to review than a whole one — the members are shared, the state machine only makes sense end to end, and the interesting rules are precisely the ones that span verbs.

## Three things these specs say that the implementation could not

**The password goes in, not out.** `initiate-export` and `finalize-import` both carry the key-derivation secret for a complete copy of an agent, *inbound*. Classified `ingests: secret` with prose forbidding logging, echoing and persisting, and the member is annotated `writeOnly` so a generated client cannot surface it in a response type.

It also gets the observation that matters to anyone building a producer: the password's exposure is decided by **where it is typed**, and no property of this protocol recovers from a field in a scriptable environment (a browser form reachable by autofill or a co-resident extension; a shell history; a CI variable). An approval ceremony guards the action, not the field. `transportToken` gets the same treatment in the other direction.

**A recipient with no address cannot export.** `initiate-export` hard-fails when the agent has no public URL — the ordinary shape for a DIDComm- or TSP-only agent, which is most of what this stack exists to support. Given a stable `transportUnavailable` code and a *Transport preconditions* section, because the producer's response to it is nothing like its response to a malformed request: this one can only be fixed by whoever configures the agent.

**Commit is deliberately not idempotent, and abort deliberately is.** Repeating an abort re-destroys something already destroyed, so making it harmless removes a race. Repeating a commit re-applies a snapshot over whatever the agent has done since — a silent rollback indistinguishable from the first success. Written down because the asymmetry reads as an inconsistency until you know why.

## Two schema decisions worth a reviewer's attention

- **No `format: "uuid"`,** though the members are UUIDs. It is the one format keyword no existing spec uses, and typify turns it into `::uuid::Uuid` — a new crate dependency for every Rust consumer of the bindings, to annotate what `pattern` already enforces. Caught by `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs`, which failed to compile.
- **No `default` on `confirm`.** A materialised default makes an omitted member indistinguishable from a deliberate one, and this is the member separating a rehearsal from an irreversible replacement. The rule is in prose with a MUST on recipients, so wire behaviour is unchanged.

## Also worth noting

`finalize-import`'s response is **counts, not contents** — deliberately. Preview runs on a bundle whose password the producer has just demonstrated they know but before the recipient commits to anything, so an inventory there would be a read of the bundle dressed as a rehearsal. `sourceDid` is the one identifier returned, because without it an operator cannot tell a right bundle from a wrong one before replacing an agent with it.

`reload-services` has an empty request payload, and the spec argues for why: every member it might carry is a way of asking the agent to run on something other than its configuration.

## Verification

- `npm run validate` — 366 specs
- `npm run check-bindings` — 366 TS and 361 Rust modules, all agree
- `npm run build-ts-bindings` + `cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen` + `cargo fmt`; `cargo fmt --check` clean
- `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --all-features` — all green
- `trust-tasks-ts`: `tsc --noEmit` clean, `npm test` 79/79
- `npm run validate-ceremonies`, `npm run test-ceremonies`

## Pre-merge checklist

- [x] Wire members are lowerCamelCase (SPEC §4.10) and match what the VTA dispatches today — `password` kept rather than renamed to `passphrase`, since renaming would be a wire break for style
- [x] Every free-text member bounded (§7.3 item 19)
- [x] Error codes lowerCamelCase and non-shadowing (§8.3)
- [x] `ext` `$ref`s `_framework/0.1/framework.schema.json#/$defs/Ext` — declared once, per the TS runtime check
- [x] `issuedAtRequirement: REQUIRED` on every consequential task (§7.3 item 17)
- [x] Security & Privacy carries all four sub-headings on all six
- [x] No specification declares a consent, approval or step-up requirement (§7.3 item 13)
- [x] `payload.invalid-examples.json` on all six, each note saying what the case protects

hard-fails when the agent has no public URL — the ordinary shape for a
DIDComm- or TSP-only agent, which is most of what this stack exists to
support. Given a stable `transportUnavailable` code and a
"Transport preconditions" section, because the producer's response to
it is nothing like its response to a malformed request: this one can
only be fixed by whoever configures the agent.

**Commit is deliberately not idempotent, and abort deliberately is.**
Repeating an abort re-destroys something already destroyed, so making
it harmless removes a race. Repeating a commit re-applies a snapshot
over whatever the agent has done since — a silent rollback that looks
identical to the first success. Written down because the asymmetry
reads as an inconsistency until you know why.

Two schema decisions worth flagging for review:

- No `format: "uuid"`, though the members are UUIDs. It is the one
  format keyword no existing spec uses, and typify turns it into
  `::uuid::Uuid` — a new crate dependency for every Rust consumer of
  the bindings, to annotate what `pattern` already enforces.
- No `default` on `confirm`. A materialised default makes an omitted
  member indistinguishable from a deliberate one, and this is the
  member separating a rehearsal from an irreversible replacement. The
  rule is in prose, with a MUST on recipients so the wire behaviour is
  unchanged.

Bindings regenerated (`build-ts-bindings`, `trust-tasks-codegen`,
`cargo fmt`); registry, bindings conformance, `cargo test --all-features`
and the TS runtime suite all pass.

title: trust-tasks-rs-v0.17.6
body:
### Added

- **rooms**: A new top-level `rooms/*` family — `create`, `records/{put,get,list}`,
  `epoch/mint`, and a `_shared` schema carrying the visibility ladder, the authority
  presentation and the sealed-record envelope.

  A **data room** is a shared space whose access is governed by credentials the room itself
  issues. The property distinguishing this family from every other stored-data task here is
  that **a host never consults a member list of its own** — which is why the family is
  top-level rather than under a service prefix. Any host that speaks it can host any room,
  and a room moves between hosts without a credential being reissued.

  Three rules are wire commitments from this first version, because retrofitting any of them
  would break every verifier:

  - **The whole authority chain is presented, leaf first, capped at 8.** A host must never
    dereference a link's `parent`: resolving over the network would make verification depend
    on availability, turn an identifier into a request the host can be induced to make
    against an address the *producer* chooses, and signal credential use to whoever hosts it.
  - **A `private` room presentation must carry `subjectBinding`** — proof that the membership
    credential and the authority chain's leaf describe the same subject. Without it two
    parties pool credentials and verify as one party holding both.
  - **Reads present exactly as writes do**, and a `private` room requires no host session.
    Authorizing reads by session would log a member identifier on every access, and a period
    of such logs reconstructs the membership the tier exists to withhold.

> **Patch, not a leading-component bump.** New spec families add modules and
> types; the generated tree carries no enum over slugs or families for a consumer
> to match exhaustively, so nothing existing stops compiling. A leading-component
> bump here would be a workspace event — seven crates pin `trust-tasks-rs = "0.17"`
> and would each need moving and releasing — for a change that breaks nobody.

- **device**: Four `Capability` values the registry was missing. `sign-trust-task`
  and `credential-write` were already served by the reference implementation
  without ever reaching the schema; `memory-read` and `memory-write` are new,
  and split a gate that was previously binary — before them, any consumer that
  could reach a trust context could also rewrite every memory in it, so there
  was no way to grant an agent read-only access to a person's memory. Added to
  both published shapes in each one's own convention: `device/_shared/0.1`
  (kebab-case) and `device/_shared/0.2` (camelCase).

> **Additive, and still a call-site break.** The generated `Capability` is a
> plain Rust enum, so four new variants make every exhaustive `match` on it
> non-exhaustive. Consumers that match with a wildcard arm are unaffected;
> consumers that enumerate need one edit each. Patch bump per this crate's
> versioning rule (the wire format is unchanged and older documents still
> parse), but worth reading before upgrading.
>
> The schema description now also states the rule consumers should already have
> been following: an unrecognised capability value is **ignored**, never treated
> as conferring anything, and never a reason to reject the whole binding.

title: feat(rooms): add the rooms/* task family
body:
**Track 2.1** of the data-rooms delivery plan. Five specs plus a shared schema:
`rooms/create`, `rooms/records/{put,get,list}`, `rooms/epoch/mint`.

## Why top-level, not under a service prefix

A **data room** is a shared space whose access is governed by credentials the *room itself*
issues. The property that distinguishes this family from every other stored-data task in the
registry is that **a host never consults a member list of its own** — authorization is a
presentation verified against the room's identifier.

That is what makes any host able to host any room, and a room able to move hosts without a
single credential being reissued. Filing it under a service prefix would encode into the URI
the one thing the design exists to avoid.

## Three wire commitments, made now because retrofitting breaks every verifier

**1. The whole chain is presented; the host never fetches.** Leaf first, capped at 8 links,
and `parent` is never dereferenced. Resolving over the network would make verification
depend on availability, turn an identifier into a request the host can be induced to make
**against an address the producer chooses**, and signal credential use to whoever hosts that
identifier. Identifiers in a chain are identifiers, not locators. The cap is a resource
bound — verification is linear and runs on every operation; known uses need 2–3.

**2. A `private` presentation MUST carry `subjectBinding`.** Proof that the membership
credential and the authority chain's leaf describe the same subject. Without it, two parties
pool credentials — one contributes membership, the other authority — and the combination
verifies as a single party holding both. Required rather than permitted, because it is
silent when wrong.

**3. Reads present exactly as writes do**, and a `private` room requires **no host session**.
Authorizing reads by session would record a member identifier on every access, and a period
of those logs reconstructs the membership the tier exists to withhold — recovered without
breaking any cryptography.

## Also carried

- **Epoch minting is restricted to `admin`.** If any key-holder could mint one, any member
  could evict any other by declining to seal them the new key — silently, with no
  server-side check possible on a room whose membership the host cannot see. Binding it to
  an action the *room* confers is what makes the restriction enforceable by a host that
  knows nothing about the membership.
- **`records/list` returns metadata, never bodies**, and returns tombstones to
  `sinceVersion` callers so deletions propagate instead of resurrecting on the next rebuild.
- **Visibility is immutable** for a room's life: a downgrade cannot un-see cleartext, and an
  upgrade would protect only what came after while presenting as though it protected
  everything.
- **The owner is visible at every visibility**, including `private`. A room whose contents
  nobody can read still has someone answerable for it existing.
- **AEAD associated data binds a record to `roomId|key|version|epoch`**, so a host that
  relocates one produces a mismatch and the open fails.

## Recipe

- `npm run validate` — **365 specs, 67 shared schemas, no errors and no warnings** (the
  `Security & Privacy` sections and their four required sub-headings are written, not
  allowlisted)
- `cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen && cargo fmt --all` — 360 payload modules
- `npm run build-ts-bindings` — 427 TS modules
- `npm run check-bindings` — *365 specifications checked against 365 TypeScript and 360 Rust modules — all agree*
- `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs` — green

## Versioning

`trust-tasks-rs` 0.17.4 → **0.18.0**, `trust-tasks-ts` 0.16.5 → **0.17.0**, in lockstep with
both CHANGELOGs and the TS lockfile. A leading-component bump: five new families reach the
generated module tree.

## Related

Implementation of the design in `OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure`
[#1233](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1233). The authority
credential these presentations carry is `dtgwg-cred-spec`
[#29](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/pull/29); the reference implementation
of chain verification is `OpenVTC/dtg-credentials`
[#15](https://github.com/OpenVTC/dtg-credentials/pull/15).

title: feat: add the VAC and VDC credential types
body:
**Track 0** of the data-rooms delivery plan. Unblocks the demo and the `rooms/*` work, and
depends on nothing — this is our library, and `DTGCredentialType` is already
`#[non_exhaustive]` with a `new_v*` constructor per type, so this is the existing pattern
rather than a fork.

Both types track drafts — `trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec`
[#29](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/pull/29) (VAC) and
[#19](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/pull/19) (VDC) — and say so in their
API docs, so a consumer knows the shape may move before those are approved.

## `authority::verify_chain` is the part that matters

Everything else here is a struct and a signature. **Anyone can mint a well-formed VAC
naming any scope and any actions, and it will verify perfectly as a credential.** What makes
it worthless is that its chain does not reach the party governing the scope — so a verifier
that checks only the credential it was handed accepts a self-issued grant of arbitrary
authority.

Seven rules, each closing one way of getting more than was granted:

| Rule | What it stops |
|---|---|
| Chain must reach a root issued by the governing party | a self-issued grant |
| No link may add an action absent from its parent | escalation by re-issue |
| No link may widen `scope` | authority earned in one room used in another |
| No link may outlive its parent | an expiry escaped by re-delegation |
| Each link's issuer must be its parent's subject | grafting someone else's grant onto your own |
| `audience`, where set, must be the presenter | a leaked credential used by whoever holds it |
| Depth bounded at 8 | DoS against a verifier that walks every link |

**Resolution is bearer-side by construction.** `verify_chain` takes the whole chain as a
slice and never dereferences `parent`. Resolving over the network would make verification
depend on availability, turn every `id` into a request the verifier can be induced to make
against an address the *holder* chooses, and signal credential use to whoever hosts the
identifier. `id` values are identifiers, not locators.

## What `attenuate` buys

The case the credential exists for: a member holds `read`/`write`/`curate` for a month;
their agent runs on `read`, for four hours, bound to the agent's own DID. Derived by the
holder with no round trip to the issuer, and refused at issue time if it would widen — while
the verifier's check remains authoritative, since nothing stops a different implementation
emitting the JSON by hand.

## Tests are mostly attacks

14 in `tests/authority_chain.rs`, and the interesting ones are the refusals: a self-issued
grant, an added action, a grafted parent, an audience-bound credential presented by someone
else, an expired link beneath a live parent, a chain past the depth ceiling, and an empty
`actions` list — which is refused **both** by the constructor and at the deserialization
boundary, since a guard only on the constructor is trivially bypassed by `serde_json`.

`cargo test` 73 passing · `cargo clippy --all-targets` clean · `cargo fmt` applied.

## Version

`0.5.0` → `0.6.0`. `DTGCredentialType` is `#[non_exhaustive]`, so callers matching with a
wildcard arm are unaffected; callers matching exhaustively need one arm each.

title: feat(example): a data room, end to end
body:
**Track 1** of the delivery plan. Stacked on
[#15](https://github.com/OpenVTC/dtg-credentials/pull/15) (the VAC/VDC types) — **review and
merge that first**; this targets that branch, and will retarget to `main` once it lands.

One example, one process, seven steps. `cargo run --example data_room`.

## What it demonstrates rather than asserts

| Step | Claim |
|---|---|
| 1 | A room is an entity — its own DID, issuing its own credentials |
| 2–3 | Joining is a **two-party act**: the VMC pair completes on Bob's acknowledgement, so a room cannot assert a membership nobody agreed to |
| 4 | Access is a chain that reaches the room. The host is not asked |
| 5 | **An agent runs on strictly less than its human** — read-only, four hours, audience-bound — and is refused `write`, which its parent holds |
| 6 | Removal actually removes: the epoch rotates, Bob's key cannot open what comes after. And forward-only is shown honestly — what he already held, he still holds |
| 7 | The host view: ciphertext, an epoch number, and nothing else |

It closes by proving a **relocated record does not open** — the AAD binding, demonstrated
rather than described.

Sample output is in the commit; the interesting lines are `agent write correctly refused:
chain does not confer action write` and `Bob's key cannot open epoch 2 — removal actually
removed`.

## Why it lives here

`examples/` rather than a new repo: it demonstrates *this* library. Its crypto is a
**dev-dependency**, so nothing in the library's own graph encrypts — adding a cipher to a
credential crate for the sake of an example would be the wrong trade.

## The one structural decision worth reviewing

The store sits behind a narrow `RoomHost` trait — `put`, `get`, `list`, `epoch`,
`set_epoch` — from the first commit. **That is the difference between this being a
foundation and being throwaway**: track 2 swaps the implementation for a VTC-backed one,
and that is only a swap if nothing above the trait reaches around it. Worth checking that
nothing does.

## What it deliberately is not

Named in the module docs against what each gap does not prove, so the demo cannot quietly
be mistaken for the product:

- **One symmetric key per epoch, not MLS** — no post-compromise security, O(n) membership change
- **`did:key`, not a witnessed `did:webvh`** — no ownership transfer
- **The `attributed` tier** — the acting member is disclosed to the host, not proven in zero knowledge
- **A `BTreeMap`, not a service** — no availability, quota, or multi-party operation

What it *does* establish is that the credential model works end to end.

title: test(vta): measure audit coverage, and close the seven silent successes
body:
Answers a question that could not be answered before: **is auditing fully implemented?**

`tests/audit_sink.rs` proves the sink *mechanism* — entries reach an installed sink rather than the keyspace. It says nothing about which tasks emit one. And the emitting is scattered by design: the spine audits the vault family centrally (`vault_audit`), everything else records in its handler, or down in `operations/`, or through the `audit!` macro. Three shapes, no index.

Grep cannot settle it — I miscounted twice before accepting that following delegation is the whole difficulty. So this is a **runtime** sweep: for every dispatched task whose declared class is not `SideEffectLevel::None`, drive it and see whether an entry appears. Request fixtures come from the conformance table, which already holds a schema-valid payload per URI.

## The headline finding: two things are called "audit"

| helper | destination |
|---|---|
| `audit!` macro | a `tracing` event on the `audit` target — **a log line** |
| `record_with_detail` | the `AuditSink` — **the queryable trail** |
| the `vta-audit` ceremony helper | both |

Nothing at the call site says which. A handler calling `audit!` alone reads as audited and is **absent from `audit/list` and from any operator's external sink**.

`session.revoke` was exactly that — `audit!("session.revoke", …)` three lines above the response, and nothing in the trail. It took a runtime sweep to notice.

That split is worth a decision beyond this PR. 36 call sites use the macro; some of those actions are *also* recorded to the sink elsewhere and some are not, and only the census can tell them apart. Happy to open an issue for consolidating the two if you want it tracked separately.

## Seven consequential tasks succeeded and recorded nothing

Now zero. Ordered by what I'd worry about:

- **`consent/approver-set`** — this binding decides *who gets asked* when a task needs a human. Moved quietly, it is the entire consent path redirected: point it at yourself and every gated action is approved by you, with the wallet still raising its prompt to somebody who never sees it. Now records, with the approver in the detail — knowing the binding changed is not enough, the reviewer needs to know what it changed *to*.
- **`keys/derive-and-sign`** and **`keys/derive-and-sign-document`** — the only signing paths that persist no key record, so without a line the signature left no evidence anywhere. The derivation path is the resource; the signed document deliberately is not recorded (it is the caller's content and may carry anything).
- `consent/revoke`, `auth/revoke-session`, `contexts/create`.

## A flaw in the census, caught before it did damage

The first version drove `dispatch_typed` rather than `dispatch_trust_task_core` — skipping the spine, which is where the vault family's central audit lives. Every `vault/*` task therefore read as silent, and I was one edit from "fixing" `vault/credentials/delete`, which had been correct all along.

The census now drives the spine, and the module header says why, so the next person does not repeat it. Worth flagging in review because it is the kind of mistake that makes a census actively harmful — a false positive here produces a "fix" to working code.

## Two ratchets, deliberately different

**Success with no trail is a hard assert.** A task that did its work and left no trace has no defensible reading, so it never gets a tolerated count.

**Audit-on-success-only is a budget** — currently **72**. These record nothing when *refused*, so a denied privileged attempt leaves no trail, and "who tried to wipe this device and was denied" is precisely the entry an incident review goes looking for. Fixing them is ~70 handlers in one diff, so the number may only shrink: lower it in the commit that fixes one, never raise it. A new handler auditing on success only is a new instance of the defect, not a reason to move the line.

Twelve consequential tasks have **no conformance fixture** and were not driven — invisible to this sweep *and* the schema one. Reported rather than asserted, since the schema sweep owns that gap. They are the `vta/backup/*`, `vta/seeds/*`, `vault/*` lifecycle and `reload-services` families, all of which are unspecced; specifying them upstream is what closes it.

## Checks

`cargo fmt --all --check`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` (no warnings), `cargo test -p vta-service --lib` — 1014 passed, and `cargo check --workspace` (CI's exact command, **not** `--all-targets`, which masked a cfg bug on a previous PR).

title: feat: replace the four VID types with a declared correlation scope (pairwise | directed | public)
body:
Implements **[#22](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/22)**, which offered to write the text if the WG considered it in scope for WD02. Here it is, so the change can be judged as spec prose rather than as a proposal.

**Updated** to carry the resolution reached in [cred-tf discussion #41](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-tf/discussions/41) and in [#22](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/22): **three** scope values, not four, and the four acronyms retired outright rather than kept as shorthand. What changed since the first push is summarised at the bottom.

## The problem

Each of the four VID types encodes **two independent things in one name**: what the identifier is attached to, and how widely it may be correlated. Only the second is what implementers and users need to reason about — and the first is already carried by the credential the identifier appears in. A VMC's subject is a member; a VRC's issuer is a party to a relationship. The credential says so.

Naming the identifier again duplicates that, and the duplication is where the ambiguity lives: put an M-DID in a VRC — which §VRC explicitly permits — and both names apply.

## The change

One axis, monotonic, declared by the holder:

| Scope | Known to | Replaces |
|---|---|---|
| `pairwise` | exactly one counterparty | R-DID; M-DID where the community is the only counterparty |
| `directed` | a set of counterparties the holder chooses | P-DID; M-DID where the member is deliberately correlatable |
| `public` | unbounded, published, meant to be found | C-DID |

Plus the principle: **roles are conferred by credentials, scope is declared by the holder.**

### Why three and not four

Per [@talltree](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/22#issuecomment-5460210235) and [@geoffturk](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/22#issuecomment-5460754153). A `community` value was the only one whose bound came from **structure** (the VMC) rather than from the holder's choice — a role smuggled back onto the scope axis, which is precisely what this change exists to remove. It is also a distinction no verifier can act on: `pairwise` is falsifiable by contradiction, `public` is observable, and everything between them is an unverifiable holder assertion, so splitting the middle gives a verifier two values it cannot tell apart.

A membership identifier is therefore `pairwise` when the community is its only counterparty, and `directed` when the member also uses it with other members. The join-time choice becomes a three-way one a person can actually be asked to make:

1. `pairwise` — known to the VTA only (**one-time pseudonym**)
2. `directed` — known to the VTA and whoever the person chooses, including other members (**private persona**)
3. `public` — known to anyone (**public persona**)

### The four acronyms are retired

Not kept as informal shorthand. R-DID / M-DID / C-DID / P-DID leave the normative model *and* the glossary; their four term files are deleted. The shorthand is where the confusion lived. The 42 dangling references this would once have created are gone — the body no longer refers to the types at all.

## What the change moves rather than removes

Three things a community-bounded scope value was quietly carrying now have explicit homes:

**1. New normative subsection — "Scope the holder cannot declare alone."** A member can declare their membership identifier `pairwise`, but that stays truthful only if the community keeps it so: a VTC that publishes a member directory, or presents a member-issued VMC to a third party (which Privacy Consideration 8 permits), has widened the exposure without the member choosing it. So: **a VTC's governance framework MUST state whether member identifiers are disclosed beyond the VTA, and to whom**, and a verifier MUST NOT infer from a member's `pairwise` declaration that the community treats it as such. This is what `community` appeared to capture — a property of the community, which belongs in its governance. A matching item is added to §Governance Considerations and to §Privacy Considerations.

**2. Intra-community relationships.** Under strict `pairwise` the identifier toward the VTC and the one toward a counterparty differ by construction, so the community-anchored ZKP must establish common control across two identifiers rather than read one out of both credentials. Stated in both §Correlation Scope and §Community-Anchored Zero-Knowledge Proof, along with the fact that `directed` is the honest default for intra-community use. The ZK protocols themselves remain out of scope, so this is not a new hole — it just stops being invisible.

**3. Durability and scope are chosen independently.** §DID Method Considerations no longer groups methods by VID type. A `pairwise` identifier toward a community must survive key rotation for the life of the membership, so "pairwise ⇒ disposable" is false. Durability follows the lifetime of the credentials issued under an identifier; scope follows the holder's disclosure choice; a method is judged against both.

## Two pieces of text delete themselves

**The uniqueness MUST becomes definitional.** §Unilateral Relationship Identification currently requires *"each entity MUST generate a new, unique R-DID for every single entity they connect with."* An identifier declared `pairwise` and then used with a second counterparty **is not pairwise** — the declaration is false. That is a more useful thing for a verifier to be able to say than a requirement it cannot check, and it makes `pairwise` the one value falsifiable on evidence. The MUST becomes a note.

**The public community stops being an anomaly.** A community that wishes to be found declares `public` and is done. No bootstrapping exception, because `public` is an ordinary value on the axis rather than a departure from a pairwise default.

## What is deliberately unchanged

**Membership is still established by the VMC pair. A persona is still asserted by the VPC.** Those mechanisms have real machinery and it is untouched. Only the claim that the identifiers are distinct *types* is retired — which is the part that collides.

Mechanically, credential field constraints reduce to plain DIDs throughout: VRC, VMC, VIC, VPC and VWC no longer name identifier types in their issuer and subject rules. One exception is stated rather than implied — a witness identifier is `directed` at minimum, since it must be recognizable to both parties to the edge and to the community whose policy it is issued under.

## One question left open on purpose

Where a declaration is *carried*. Two placements are viable and the choice has consequences:

1. **In the credential, by the party whose identifier it is.** Bidirectional edges make this complete on their own — in a VMC pair the community declares its own scope in the grant and the member declares theirs in the acknowledgement, so each half carries a first-party declaration.
2. **In the DID document**, resolved with the identifier.

The first keeps the declaration signed by the party it describes and needs no resolution step; the second states scope once rather than per credential, but puts it where a verifier must fetch it and whoever hosts the document can watch that fetch.

**The vocabulary and the principle can be adopted independently of the carriage.** Implementer input on placement specifically requested.

## Changed since the first push

- `community` dropped; `linked` renamed `directed` — per #41 and [#22](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/22#issuecomment-5460754153).
- The four acronyms retired outright; `relationship_did.md`, `membership_did.md`, `community_did.md` and `persona_did.md` deleted rather than rewritten as shorthand.
- Added §Choosing a scope (informative — the three-way HTX choice, and when intentional correlation needs a ZK proof at all, per [@talltree](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/22#issuecomment-5465297803)).
- Added §Scope the holder cannot declare alone (normative — the VTC disclosure requirement), with matching Governance and Privacy items.
- Added the durability-vs-scope rule to §DID Method Considerations.
- Credential field constraints reduced to plain DIDs; witness identifier stated as `directed` at minimum.
- Privacy Consideration 1 (M-DID reuse / migration) deleted; a new item covers what a community does with a member's identifier.
- `CONTEXT.md` updated so the repo's own vocabulary note no longer teaches the four types.

Spec-Up-T renders clean with no dangling references introduced.

## Related

- Implements [#22](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/22) — the structural proposal; carries the three-value resolution reached there.
- Carries the naming resolution from [dtgwg-cred-tf#41](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-tf/discussions/41).
- Resolves [#21](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/21) — the glossary/body contradiction over VRC edge verifiability was a symptom of the same double-naming; the VRC glossary entry no longer types the identifiers. [#26](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/pull/26) states the conditions normatively and the two need reconciling on merge.
- Answers [#23](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/23) — an asymmetric edge is nameable once each half declares its own scope; §Scope the holder cannot declare alone states that a declaration binds only its own holder. [#27](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/pull/27) adds the max-of-halves rule and is unaffected by the reduction to three values.
- Supersedes the C-DID amendment in [#29](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/pull/29) and resolves its service-identifier editor's note — under a scope axis a mediator's identifier is simply `public`, with no new type needed. The two are otherwise independent.
- Independent of [#28](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/28), which reorders the credential-category sections. No overlap in substance — this PR does not touch the taxonomy — but both edit `spec/body.md` in the same neighbourhood, so whichever merges second will need a textual rebase.

title: feat: add the VAC (verifiable authority credential)
body:
Raised as a **draft for discussion** — the category question in §Authority is
not delegation is deliberately left to the WG.

## The gap

The catalog has six credentials and **none of them confers authority**. Two
build edges (VMC, VRC), one invites (VIC), three annotate (VPC, VEC, VWC). There
is no credential whose meaning is *"the holder may do X here"*.

So implementations reach for the nearest thing and pack permission into a VEC —
`endorsement: { type: "CommunityRole", role: … }` is already in the wild. That
near-miss is the argument for this PR: **an endorsement is a statement *about* a
party**, which a verifier weighs for itself. **An authority credential is a
statement *to* a verifier**: the party governing the scope has decided.
Conflating them puts a decision belonging to the governing party into a claim
that reads as reputation, and leaves verifiers inferring permission from
adjectives.

## What this adds

A fourth functional category (**Authority Credentials**) and the **VAC**: an
issuer that governs a scope, a subject, and the named actions they may take
within it. An empty `actions` array confers nothing rather than everything —
emptiness is never a wildcard.

**Attenuation is the part that earns its place.** A holder may derive a narrower
VAC from one they already hold, without involving the issuer: fewer actions, no
later expiry, no wider scope, optionally bound to an `audience` that must be the
presenter.

The case that forces it is the **AI agent**. A person's agent should carry four
hours of read-only access to one scope — not the person's own standing
authority. There is currently no way to express that in this catalog, and the
alternative in practice is agents running as their humans.

Verifiers MUST walk the chain to a VAC issued by the governing party and reject
any link that widens. Verifying only the presented credential accepts a
self-issued grant of arbitrary authority, so this is stated normatively in
§Attenuation, in Security Considerations, and in Conformance Targets.

## Two normative rules worth reviewing closely

**Authority is not delegation.** A VAC authorizes acting *in one's own name*
within a scope — never *on behalf of* another party. These are different
questions (*may this party do this here?* vs *may this party stand in for that
one?*) and answering both with one credential means a verifier cannot tell which
it has been shown. A companion **VDC** covering acting-on-behalf-of is proposed
separately; an editor's note leaves the category question — whether the VDC
joins `Authority Credentials` or warrants its own — to the WG once both are
before it, rather than pre-empting it here. The categories are informative
groupings, so this does not affect either schema.

**Authority and membership stay separate credentials** — and where both are
proven in zero knowledge with the subject withheld, the presentation MUST prove
they share a subject. Without it, two parties pool credentials: one contributes
membership, the other authority, and the combination verifies as a single party
holding both. This is easy to miss in implementation and silent when wrong, so
it is normative in the VAC section, cross-referenced from Zero-Knowledge and
Selective Disclosure, and listed in Security Considerations.

## Also resolves an existing editor's note

The VIC section asks *"whether any of this [role and access control] information
should be embedded in the VIC itself"*. This PR answers it: **no** — what a
party may *do* is conferred by a VAC, which can be reissued or attenuated
without touching the invitation that admitted them. The note is updated to
record the answer rather than the question.

## Changes

- `spec/body.md` — new `## Authority Credentials` section (VAC schema, two
  examples, attenuation rules, the two normative rules above); taxonomy diagram
  and formal type hierarchy; Security Considerations; Conformance Targets; ZKP
  predicate list; VIC editor's note.
- `spec/intro.md`, `spec/header.md` — six → seven types, three → four categories.
- `spec/terms-definitions/verifiable_authority_credential.md` — new term.

All `[[ref:]]` references resolve against existing or added definitions.

title: Add a privacy consideration for the effective disclosure of an edge
body:
Addresses #23. One paragraph, one file.

The rule proposed in #23 and supported by both @mitchuski and @albertoleon7794: **a choice of identifier constrains only its own holder's disclosure, and an edge's effective disclosure is the wider of its two halves.**

## Why it is missing today

Privacy consideration 2 covers R-DID reuse — an issuer's own failure, which the issuer can avoid. This is the other case: a *correctly* unique R-DID that is correlated to a named party because the counterparty published the opposing half under an M-DID into a readable graph. The party who loses privacy is the one who followed the specification's recommendation, through an action it neither controls nor can discover. Nothing currently warns an implementation that computing an edge's privacy from the half it issued gives the wrong answer.

## Two corrections to the framing in #23

I filed #23 as a cross-community problem. Two people have since improved on that, and the text reflects them rather than my original framing:

- @albertoleon7794's classifier returns **no answer** — not a wrong one — when asked whether a mixed edge is an R-DID or an M-DID edge, and, more usefully, showed the same failure is reachable **inside a single community** passing through the migration consideration 1 recommends. So it is not a cross-community special case, and the text says so.
- @mitchuski's observer reading generalises past two-party edges, so the paragraph closes on joint presentation: what a set of credentials discloses together may exceed what any of them discloses alone.

## Scope

Stated as a consideration rather than a normative requirement: it describes a property an implementation must compute correctly, not behaviour a credential can be checked against.

Written to stand **independently of #22**. If the declared-scope model lands, this falls out of the vocabulary and the paragraph can be shortened to the one-line rule; until then it needs saying in prose. It also does not depend on #26.

`npm run render` clean, dangling-definitions list unchanged from `main`.
