body:
### Fixed

- **sdk**: Give every authenticated client its identity, and adopt provision/integration 0.3 ([#1147](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1147))

#1146 made every producer sign, and left seven production paths building
  clients that cannot. Each authenticates, takes the token, and drops the DID and
  key on the floor — so every task they dispatch is refused for a missing
  `recipient` and `proof`. `SessionStore::connect` was fixed; nothing else was,
  because no test drives those paths against an enforcing VTA.

- **vta**: Re-case the extended error codes the Trust Tasks registry moved ([#1122](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1122))

* fix(vta)!: emit the re-cased extended error codes the registry now declares

  trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#279 re-cased 200 extended error-code local
  parts to lowerCamelCase per SPEC §4.10 rule 4 — only the part after the `:`
  moved, the namespace is unchanged. This service still produced the snake_case
  spellings for 32 of them, so every one of those rejects carried a code the
  registry no longer defines and no conforming consumer can branch on.

  Every site here is an **emitter**: this repo decides what to send, and the
  registry decides what is correct to send, so each moves to the new spelling
  with no compatibility arm. The matcher side — where this repo reads a code a
  peer produced and cannot control that peer's deploy order — is handled
  separately in the following commit.

  Three of the vault emitters build their namespace by interpolation
  (`vault/{verb}:not_found`, `vault/{verb}:version_conflict`,
  `vault/{op}:not_found` in `vault_not_found`, `check_expected_version` and
  `refuse_if_not_active`), so the codes they produce do not appear as literals
  anywhere. Those helpers cover `vault/delete:{notFound,versionConflict}` and the
  `notFound` conflation the three consumer-facing use paths rely on for
  enumeration resistance.



### Chore

- **sdk**: Release vta-sdk 0.30.0 for the added CreateKeyBody field ([#1156](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1156))

`CreateKeyBody` gained a `key_id` field while the crate stayed at 0.29.0.
  The struct is exhaustively constructible through the public API, so an
  existing literal no longer compiles — a breaking change under 0.x rules,
  which the semver report has been flagging as its one real finding
  (195 pass, 1 fail) since the field landed.

  Bumps the crate and the nineteen intra-workspace requirements that pin it,
  so `cargo check --workspace` still resolves the path copy and a consumer
  resolving from the registry gets a version that admits the break.

title: test(vta): census the URIs this service produces, not just the ones it serves
body:
Second half of #1177 — the structural fix, so the next inline-constructed outbound document is visible the day it lands rather than years later.

### The hole

Three harnesses police the task surface, and a document can slip between all three:

| harness | why it missed the consent prompt |
|---|---|
| `UNSPECCED_DISPATCHED_URIS` | per-URI and shrink-only, but tracks what the dispatcher **serves** |
| `producer_payload_conformance` | drives client methods; this is built inline, through no `VtaClient` method |
| VTC manifest census | its `PREFIX` is `https://trusttasks.org/openvtc/vtc/`, the VTC's *private* namespace — a public `spec/` URI never matches it wherever it runs |

That last one matters: an earlier read of this suggested adding `vta-service/src` to that census's `BINDING_SITES` would fix it. It wouldn't have.

So: **serving** an unspecced URI fails the build; **producing** one was invisible. That's why `consent/approve-request/0.1` shipped unsigned for as long as it did.

### What this adds

Every `https://trusttasks.org/spec/...` literal under `vta-service/src` must be published, served (where the other harness owns the debt), or listed with a reason. Shrink-only in both directions, matching the served-side list.

### It found two on day one

`vta/attestation/{status,report}/1.0` are **REST-routed rather than dispatched**, so the served-URI harness never saw them. `status` is unauthenticated and internet-reachable — the thing a verifier checks *before* deciding to trust this VTA at all, and the one surface here whose counterparty isn't the operator. Both recorded against #1177.

### Three exclusions, each stated rather than silently skipped

- `format!` templates carrying `{version}`, and prefix constants ending in `/` — neither is a URI that goes on a wire.
- The **`trust-task-error/*` family**, which *is* in the registry (`/0.1` … `/0.5`) but for which `schema_for` answers `None`, because `schema_index` carries payload schemas for *tasks*. Using that as the published-check would report a published document as debt.
- Negative fixtures, as an **explicit list rather than a heuristic**. Inferring "is this inside a test module" from source text would be wrong occasionally and silently, and this only works if a failure means something.

### Verified by mutation, not assumed

- Renaming the produced consent URI → census fails, naming the new URI.
- Adding an already-published URI to the tracked list → shrink guard fails.

`cargo clippy -p vta-service --all-features --all-targets` → 0; 974 lib tests pass.

Refs #1177.

title: vti-common-v0.15.0
body:
### Added

- **vtc**: State artifact lifecycle precedence once, and apply it on read ([#1179](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1179))
- **tasks**: Catch up to the registry on vault 0.3, device/wipe 0.2 and credentials/issue 0.2 ([#1145](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1145))

Five of the six families vta-sdk lagged the registry on. The sixth,
  `provision/integration/0.3`, is not here: its response schema could never
  validate — `required` named a `digest` the 0.2→0.3 rename had already removed
  from `properties`, against `additionalProperties: false`. Fixed upstream in
  trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#324; VTI adopts it once that publishes.

  **vault/{list,get,upsert} 0.3.** `AttachmentRef.sha256` — hex, with SHA-256
  pinned by an `^[0-9a-f]{64}$` pattern — becomes `digestMultibase`, a multibase
  multihash that names its own algorithm. Worth stating plainly: nothing in this
  service has ever constructed an `AttachmentRef`. Every site is `vec![]` and
  `vault/upsert` only carries forward whatever an entry already had, so the
  member has never reached the wire and this is a type-level rename today. The
  wire contract is what changes, and it changes so that moving off SHA-256 later
  is a value change rather than another schema revision.

  **device/wipe 0.2.** `cache-and-keys` → `cacheAndKeys`, the same recasing the
  rest of the device slice took. Its constant carried "No 0.2 spec exists
  upstream; this stays on 0.1" while `specs/device/wipe/0.2` had been published
  for some time. The replacement comment says so: a comment asserting an absence
  is a claim about the registry that nothing re-checks, and it is why nobody
  looked again.

  **vta/credentials/issue 0.2.** The request payload is unchanged. The response
  stops restating the shared `IssuedCredential` inline and composes it through
  `allOf` + `unevaluatedProperties` — same members, same required set, identical
  wire form. So the two versions share a dispatch arm rather than a transform.

  The edge-transform table goes from one wire URI per spec to a list.
  `vault/*` 0.3 differs from 0.2 only in `AttachmentRef`, which is not an enum
  value and not at any path the transform touches — so it down-converts to the
  same canonical handler by the same casing rules. Giving it its own row would
  have duplicated every path and left the two to be kept in step by hand.

  `upconvert_response` now answers as the version the caller *sent*. With several
  wire URIs per spec, retyping a response to a fixed one would be refused by a
  client validating against the version it asked for.

  Two guards needed widening, and both were right to fail first:

  * `superseded_tasks_are_dispatched` did not count an edge-transformed URI as
    served. Its premise is that a row whose counter can never move reads the same
    as "safe to retire" — but the counter *does* move for these, because
    `dispatch_trust_task_core` reads the superseded row from the URI as it
    arrived, before the down-convert. The successor half of the pair already
    accepted them.
  * the wire/deprecation parity test checked only the 0.1 hop. A spec accepting
    0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 needs a row per superseded version, or the middle one is
    retired on no evidence at all.

  `ALL_URIS` and `retry_safety` carry the four new URIs; the census caught their
  absence, which is what it is for.

- **vta**: Stop error messages from being a probing oracle ([#1130](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1130))

Framework 0.5.0 makes the message-sanitization rule normative for every code,
  not just `identityMismatch`: a `message` MUST NOT reveal consumer-internal
  state, the contested value of a mismatched party, or resolver, verifier, or
  key-status internals. Every rejection is emitted on the same path, to the same
  possibly-unauthenticated party, generally before any authorization decision has
  been reached.

  This service violated two of the three.

  `app_error_to_reject` passed `AppError::Internal`'s cause into the `message`
  verbatim, so a caller learned "ATM not configured — server cannot pack DIDComm
  envelopes" or "log entry has no update_keys" — the deployment's shape, its
  configuration, and which invariant just broke. The catch-all arm was the
  quieter half: it rendered whatever `Display` an error happened to have, so a
  variant added later would publish itself with nobody choosing to. Both now land
  on one fixed string and log the cause for the operator.

  `DiProofError`'s `Display` rendered the underlying verifier error, and that
  reaches the wire through `PermissionDenied`. A caller could read which
  cryptosuite ran and how verification failed. The detail moves to a `cause()`
  that is deliberately not reachable through `Display`, since the defect was that
  the wire rendering and the operator rendering were one function.

  `notFound`, `malformedRequest` and `permissionDenied` pass through unchanged:
  they describe the caller's own request back to it, which is not
  consumer-internal state.

  `an_internal_error_does_not_say_internal_error_twice` asserted the cause was on
  the wire. Its subject was a doubled prefix, which the fixed string also
  settles; it is now `an_internal_error_reveals_no_internal_state`, joined by
  `the_catch_all_arm_is_opaque_too`.



### Chore

- **deps**: Aes-gcm 0.11, and stop the nonce conversions panicking ([#1173](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1173))
- **sdk**: Release vta-sdk 0.30.0 for the added CreateKeyBody field ([#1156](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1156))

`CreateKeyBody` gained a `key_id` field while the crate stayed at 0.29.0.
  The struct is exhaustively constructible through the public API, so an
  existing literal no longer compiles — a breaking change under 0.x rules,
  which the semver report has been flagging as its one real finding
  (195 pass, 1 fail) since the field landed.

  Bumps the crate and the nineteen intra-workspace requirements that pin it,
  so `cargo check --workspace` still resolves the path copy and a consumer
  resolving from the registry gets a version that admits the break.

title: vta-sdk-v0.31.0
body:
### Added

- **credentials**: Move vta/credentials/issue to 0.2 ([#1159](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1159))

The last family behind its latest published spec. Checked against
  `website/registry.json` rather than the schema files on disk: every other
  implemented family is already on the newest published version.

  0.1 and 0.2 have identical payloads. The response differs only in how it is
  written — 0.2 composes it from `credentials/_shared/0.2`'s
  `IssuedCredentialBase` instead of restating the members inline, which is
  what stops the two drifting. The composition brings one new member,
  `issuedAt`.

  That member costs nothing to fill: `IssuedCredentialRecord` has carried
  `issued_at` since the family existed, and 0.1 simply had nowhere to put it,
  so the value was being computed, stored, and then dropped on the way out.
  It stays `Option` on our side because the shared definition declares it
  optional — a response without it is schema-valid and must still
  deserialize — but the VTA always sends it.

  The conformance sweep caught something on the way through, which is what it
  is for. Its drifted-witness check asserts the generated type rejects an
  unknown member, and 0.2's response type does not: closing a composed object
  requires `unevaluatedProperties` (`additionalProperties` is evaluated
  per-subschema and would reject the `allOf`-supplied members), and
  trust-tasks-codegen maps only `additionalProperties: false` onto
  `deny_unknown_fields`. So the generated struct is permissive where 0.1's
  was strict.

  The wire is unaffected — the schema itself is strict, so `validate_payload`
  still rejects the member. What is lost is the type-level guard, which makes
  the drifted-witness check pass vacuously. Recorded in
  `PERMISSIVE_GENERATED_TYPE` with its reason and skipped rather than left to
  give false assurance. The fix belongs in the codegen; deleting the entry
  re-arms the check.

Each authenticates, takes the token, and drops the DID and key on the floor — so every task they dispatch is refused for a missing `recipient` and `proof`. `SessionStore::connect` was fixed; nothing else was, because no test drives those paths against an enforcing VTA. - **vta**: Re-case the extended error codes the Trust Tasks registry moved ([#1122](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1122)) * fix(vta)!: emit the re-cased extended error codes the registry now declares trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#279 re-cased 200 extended error-code local parts to lowerCamelCase per SPEC §4.10 rule 4 — only the part after the `:` moved, the namespace is unchanged. This service still produced the snake_case spellings for 32 of them, so every one of those rejects carried a code the registry no longer defines and no conforming consumer can branch on. Every site here is an **emitter**: this repo decides what to send, and the registry decides what is correct to send, so each moves to the new spelling with no compatibility arm. The matcher side — where this repo reads a code a peer produced and cannot control that peer's deploy order — is handled separately in the following commit. Three of the vault emitters build their namespace by interpolation (`vault/{verb}:not_found`, `vault/{verb}:version_conflict`, `vault/{op}:not_found` in `vault_not_found`, `check_expected_version` and `refuse_if_not_active`), so the codes they produce do not appear as literals anywhere. Those helpers cover `vault/delete:{notFound,versionConflict}` and the `notFound` conflation the three consumer-facing use paths rely on for enumeration resistance. ### Chore - **sdk**: Release vta-sdk 0.30.0 for the added CreateKeyBody field ([#1156](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1156)) `CreateKeyBody` gained a `key_id` field while the crate stayed at 0.29.0. The struct is exhaustively constructible through the public API, so an existing literal no longer compiles — a breaking change under 0.x rules, which the semver report has been flagging as its one real finding (195 pass, 1 fail) since the field landed. Bumps the crate and the nineteen intra-workspace requirements that pin it, so `cargo check --workspace` still resolves the path copy and a consumer resolving from the registry gets a version that admits the break.
## `vta-audit`
## [0.3.0](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/compare/vta-audit-v0.2.0...vta-audit-v0.3.0) — 2026-08-28 ### Added - **audit**: Bound the operator reason an audit row keeps ([#1132](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1132)) Framework 0.5.0 requires every free-text member to carry a bound. Most of that is upstream schema work, but one free-text path is this workspace's own and was bounded by nothing: the operator `reason` that `record_with_detail` writes into the audit log. The cost here is worse than the wire cost 0.5.0 argues from. The row goes into a hash-chained, append-only log, so an oversized `detail` is permanent and cannot be trimmed later without breaking the chain that makes the log evidence. Truncated at 4096 characters rather than rejected, and that choice is the substance: this runs after the operation it records has already happened, so refusing the row would trade an over-long reason for no audit record at all — losing the evidence to protect its formatting. The cut is marked, because a silently shortened reason reads as the operator's own words. Cut on a character boundary: byte-slicing panics mid-codepoint, and would do so on the first operator who wrote a reason in a language this workspace did not anticipate. The rest of the free-text rule is upstream and already in hand: 1013 of 1067 registry free-text members carry no maxLength, and dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#296 is open across 275 files to fix exactly that. Taking the latest trust-tasks-rs today would not bound free text — 0.14.0 predates it. ### Chore - **sdk**: Release vta-sdk 0.30.0 for the added CreateKeyBody field ([#1156](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1156)) `CreateKeyBody` gained a `key_id` field while the crate stayed at 0.29.0. The composition brings one new member, `issuedAt`. That member costs nothing to fill: `IssuedCredentialRecord` has carried `issued_at` since the family existed, and 0.1 simply had nowhere to put it, so the value was being computed, stored, and then dropped on the way out. It stays `Option` on our side because the shared definition declares it optional — a response without it is schema-valid and must still deserialize — but the VTA always sends it. The conformance sweep caught something on the way through, which is what it is for. Its drifted-witness check asserts the generated type rejects an unknown member, and 0.2's response type does not: closing a composed object requires `unevaluatedProperties` (`additionalProperties` is evaluated per-subschema and would reject the `allOf`-supplied members), and trust-tasks-codegen maps only `additionalProperties: false` onto `deny_unknown_fields`. The fix belongs in the codegen; deleting the entry re-arms the check. - **compliance**: Enforce SPEC §7.2's flag-driven checks, and sign what we send ([#1146](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1146)) The VTA enforced none of the four checks a *Trust Task specification* declares for itself. That is what makes the check reachable at all: `enforce_spec_policy` reads them off `P`, and the dispatch spine holds a `TrustTask`. The alternative was a 109-entry URI→type table in this repo, duplicating what the codegen already emits. The spine's own comment claimed "each slice's typed handler runs it after `parse_payload`". No handler did — that comment was the only occurrence of `enforce_audience_binding` in the repository. **This is an auth-model change, not a wire-format one.** A bearer token authenticates the connection; §7.2 item 7 admits no transport substitute, so every producer must now sign every document. `vta-sdk` gains `ClientIdentity` (client DID, its key, the VTA's DID) and signs in `dispatch_trust_task`. `SessionStore::connect` supplies it from the stored session — re-read *after* `ensure_authenticated`, because a session that needed rotation now holds a different DID and key, and signing with the pre-rotation pair produces a document whose issuer no longer matches the identity its token authenticates. `issuer` and `recipient` are set in `build_task_document` rather than at each call site, for the reason `issuedAt` already was: a member the framework requires of every document belongs to the one function that builds every document. Signing is unconditional rather than keyed on the flag — a proof on a task that merely RECOMMENDs one is legal and strictly more attributable — but it must never happen without an in-band recipient, and both come from the same `ClientIdentity` so they cannot come apart. Test identities are now derived from one-byte seeds. `did:key:zTestAdmin` was not a `did:key`: nothing resolves it and no document issued by it can carry a verifiable proof. That was fine while proofless documents were accepted. The seed gives a DID and the key behind it from one place, which is what item 6 needs — it rejects a document whose in-band issuer disagrees with the transport-authenticated identity, so a test minting a token for one DID and signing with another is refused for that rather than for what it meant to check. This service had a live instance. A policy denial puts the Rego module's `explanation` on the wire, and that string is authored by whoever wrote the policy with no length anybody checked. The bound is 4096 bytes of JCS or 16 immediate members — 0.5.0's default where a specification declares none — applied in `reject_with`, the single funnel every rejection passes through, rather than at the thirty `details: Some(...)` construction sites. An oversized `details` is ignored and never grounds to discard the `code`: the code is what the receiving party needs, and dropping the rejection because its annex was too long would turn a verbose policy into an unexplained failure. An uncanonicalisable `details` is dropped too — it cannot be measured, so it does not go out. - **vta**: Stop error messages from being a probing oracle ([#1130](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1130)) Framework 0.5.0 makes the message-sanitization rule normative for every code, not just `identityMismatch`: a `message` MUST NOT reveal consumer-internal state, the contested value of a mismatched party, or resolver, verifier, or key-status internals. Every rejection is emitted on the same path, to the same possibly-unauthenticated party, generally before any authorization decision has been reached. This service violated two of the three. `app_error_to_reject` passed `AppError::Internal`'s cause into the `message` verbatim, so a caller learned "ATM not configured — server cannot pack DIDComm envelopes" or "log entry has no update_keys" — the deployment's shape, its configuration, and which invariant just broke. The catch-all arm was the quieter half: it rendered whatever `Display` an error happened to have, so a variant added later would publish itself with nobody choosing to. Both now land on one fixed string and log the cause for the operator. `DiProofError`'s `Display` rendered the underlying verifier error, and that reaches the wire through `PermissionDenied`. A caller could read which cryptosuite ran and how verification failed. Its subject was a doubled prefix, which the fixed string also settles; it is now `an_internal_error_reveals_no_internal_state`, joined by `the_catch_all_arm_is_opaque_too`. - **vta**: Bound the replay record by the acceptance window, not by capacity ([#1127](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1127)) The follow-up #1126 named. VTI now honours SPEC §7.2's same-bound rule: the acceptance window and the duplicate-execution record's retention are one instant, derived from one policy. #1126 shipped the ReplayGuard without a window, leaving the record bounded by InMemoryReplayGuard's capacity. That is not "no expiry so entries live forever" — it is LRU, which makes the window load-dependent: on a quiet service the protection is effectively unbounded, but under burst the eviction horizon can fall below any sensible acceptance window and a replay executes a second time. The defence was weakest exactly when the service was busiest. Ten minutes rather than the library's five: this service routes over a mediator that can hold a message while a recipient reconnects. It is the same 600s the retired replay::check_and_record used as its dedup TTL, now bounding acceptance as well as retention. Most of the diff is the fixture migration the window forced, and none of it was the policy being wrong. 65 envelopes carried no issuedAt at all — with a window set, a document with neither issuedAt nor expiresAt cannot be placed in time and is refused, which is what §7.2 requires. 12 more carried fixed literals already days stale. One subtlety: the first pass used to_rfc3339(), which renders the offset as +00:00 where TrustTask's typed DateTime round-trip renders Z. That broke a signed fixture's proof — a document signed in one spelling and verified after the other is a different document, which is the §8.4 distinction #1126 added idConflict for, arriving as a signature failure instead. Every stamp now uses to_rfc3339_opts(SecondsFormat::Secs, true). - **vta**: Adopt ReplayGuard and FreshnessPolicy, deleting the hand-rolled pair ([#1126](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1126)) The last of the three stopgaps #1121 unblocked. Deletes trust_tasks/replay.rs and the hand-rolled freshness bounds from #1117. They land together because ConsumeChecks bundles them in one argument: SPEC §7.2 makes the acceptance window and the replay record's retention the same bound, and splitting them is how a deployment ends up with a ten-minute record against an unbounded window believing it has a replay defence. This service had exactly that. The retired module keyed on (actor, id) and kept no digest, which cost two things. It never produced idConflict — item 11 requires a different document under an accepted id to be rejected, and with no digest that case was silently absorbed as a retry, the one outcome §7.2 and §8.4 both rule out. And the key was wrong: §7.2 fixes it as the document id alone, so actor-scoping let two callers each spend the same id. A duplicate is also no longer answered with taskFailed, which §7.2 forbids outright. A failed outcome releases the claim, mirroring the idempotency layer beside it; a successful one records its response so a retry is answered with the result. The Err arm fails closed with a retryable unavailable, and the non_exhaustive ReplayVerdict gets an arm that refuses rather than executes. No acceptance window yet, and that was measured rather than assumed: with_max_age(10 minutes) scoped to consequential tasks failed 41 assertions across 10 suites with expired, because the suite is full of documents stamped hours or days in the past. Fixing those alters what the service accepts and belongs in a change whose subject is the window. ### Fixed - **consent**: Sign the approve-request prompt sent to an approver's device ([#1180](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1180)) `consent/approve-request/0.1` was constructed as a bare `id` / `type` / `issuedAt` / `payload` document and buffered to an approver's mediator for delivery to their phone, where a human is asked to approve something. It carried no proof, so nothing the device could check authenticated it. This is the odd one out rather than a deliberate exception. The sibling task-consent request in `consent_request.rs` already signs with this key and cryptosuite, and the step-up prompt's mobile parser refuses to render without a verified proof from an enrolled issuer (`vta-mobile-core::task::parse_step_up_request` — "no valid proof from an enrolled executor, no prompt"). Both end up in front of a person. `issuer` and `recipient` come with the proof, not as decoration: SPEC §7.2 item 5b makes `recipient` REQUIRED and item 6 requires the in-band issuer to match the transport identity. A proof over a document naming neither party is replayable at a different approver, which is most of what the signature was supposed to buy. Fails closed. The wake path is best-effort and already warns on a failed buffer, leaving the approver to mediator pickup; an unsignable prompt takes the same route. "No prompt" is recoverable in a way "unverifiable prompt" is not.
## `vtc-client`
## [0.5.0](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/compare/vtc-client-v0.4.0...vtc-client-v0.5.0) — 2026-08-28 ### Chore - **sdk**: Release vta-sdk 0.30.0 for the added CreateKeyBody field ([#1156](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1156)) `CreateKeyBody` gained a `key_id` field while the crate stayed at 0.29.0. The struct is exhaustively constructible through the public API, so an existing literal no longer compiles — a breaking change under 0.x rules, which the semver report has been flagging as its one real finding (195 pass, 1 fail) since the field landed. Bumps the crate and the nineteen intra-workspace requirements that pin it, so `cargo check --workspace` still resolves the path copy and a consumer resolving from the registry gets a version that admits the break.

title: fix(consent)!: sign the approve-request prompt sent to an approver's device
body:
First half of #1177.

`consent/approve-request/0.1` was constructed as a bare document and buffered to an approver's mediator for delivery to their phone, where a human is asked to approve something:

```rust
let approve_request = serde_json::json!({
    "id": format!("urn:uuid:{}", Uuid::new_v4()),
    "type": CONSENT_APPROVE_REQUEST_TYPE,
    "issuedAt": chrono::Utc::now().to_rfc3339_opts(chrono::SecondsFormat::Secs, true),
    "payload": prompt_payload,
});
```

No proof. Nothing the device could check authenticated it.

**This is the odd one out, not a deliberate exception.** The sibling task-consent request in `consent_request.rs` already signs with this key and cryptosuite. The step-up prompt's mobile parser refuses to render without a verified proof from an enrolled issuer — `vta-mobile-core/src/task.rs:93`, *"The gate: no valid proof from an enrolled executor, no prompt."* Both paths end up in front of a person being asked to authorise something; only one was authenticated.

### `issuer` and `recipient` come with it

Not decoration. SPEC §7.2 item 5b makes `recipient` REQUIRED and item 6 requires the in-band issuer to match the transport identity. A proof over a document naming neither party is replayable at a different approver — which is most of what the signature was supposed to buy.

### Fails closed

The wake path is best-effort and already warns on a failed buffer, leaving the approver to mediator pickup. An unsignable prompt takes the same route rather than going out unsigned: "no prompt" is recoverable in a way "unverifiable prompt" is not.

### Sequencing — why now rather than later

**This changes nothing about security on its own**, because nothing verifies it yet. That is precisely the reason to land it in this release: the fleet has to be *signing* before devices can *require* a signature. Device-side enforcement in `vta-mobile-core` follows, and must not ship first or it breaks every VTA that has not deployed this. Publishing the spec with `proof` REQUIRED is the third step.

### On the test

It runs the real verifier over the document as sent, rather than asserting a `proof` member exists — a signature copied from another document would satisfy the weaker check. It also pins `issuer` and `recipient`. I confirmed it has teeth by swapping the recipient DID for a different one and watching it fail.

Verified: `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets` → 0; `cargo test -p vta-service --all-features` passes; the `didcomm`-without-`webvh` combination (which this code path has broken before) builds.

title: release(core): @openvtc/pnm-core 0.6.0
body:
npm has served 0.5.0 since earlier today, which predates #131 — the change that made every channel sign the document it sends.

## Why the leading component moves

The runtime export diff against the published 0.5.0 tarball is **additive**: 214 exports against 213, one added (`signOutboundTask`), none removed.

The break is not a removal but a **new required input** — `signing: SigningIdentity` on `RestChannel`, `TspChannel`, `DidcommVtaTransport`, and the eleven `*RestOptions` bags that construct a channel for the caller. A TypeScript consumer gets a compile error; a JavaScript consumer gets a throw at send time. Either way existing calling code stops, which is what the version is for.

Required rather than optional is deliberate, and the Migration section leads with why: a channel constructible without a signer is a channel that silently sends unsigned documents, and that failure surfaces only as a `proofRequired` refusal from the agent — at which point nothing local identifies which call site forgot.

## Contents

- `@openvtc/pnm-core` → 0.6.0; `packages/extension` and `packages/pwa` pins → `^0.6.0` (their `^0.5.0` would not have resolved to it).
- Changelog: the empty `[Unreleased]` becomes `[0.6.0]`, with Migration / Fixed / Added / Changed covering #131 and the `@openvtc/trust-tasks` 0.16.3 bump.

No source changes — this is the version bump and changelog only.

## Verification

- `npm run clean --workspace @openvtc/pnm-core` then `tsc -b` — **not** a bare `rm -rf dist`, which leaves the `.tsbuildinfo` and makes the next build report success while emitting nothing.
- All 591 tests pass across the four workspaces.
- Each of the 23 declared `exports` entry points exists in the built `dist`.
- `npm pack --dry-run`: 478 files, 339.8 kB packed.

Publishing happens from `main` after merge (`npm publish --workspace @openvtc/pnm-core --access public`), and needs the browser OTP.

## Pre-merge checklist

- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2) — n/a, no source change
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3) — n/a
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1) — n/a
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4) — n/a
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5) — n/a
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6) — n/a
- [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, deny_unknown_fields where security-relevant, schema registered, all consumers (incl. JS) updated (R3.*) — no wire change
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive; fail-closed if enforcement can't start (R5.*) — n/a
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified; background-job failures are surfaced (R6.*) — n/a
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1) — n/a
- [x] Deviations from this guide flagged explicitly with rule numbers — none

title: fix(core)!: sign every outbound Trust-Task document, at the channel (#131)
body:
fix(core)!: sign every outbound Trust-Task document, at the channel (#131)

VTI #1146 turned on the four checks a Trust Task specification declares for
itself, on the dispatch spine common to all three transports. Three of them
this wallet already satisfied — `recipient`, `issuedAt`, audience binding. The
fourth it did not.

**93 of the 141 task types this wallet speaks declare `proof` REQUIRED** (SPEC
§7.2 item 7a) — every `vault/*`, `acl/*`, `vta/webvh/*`, `credential-exchange/*`
and `vtc/*` mutation among them. `signTrustTask` was called in exactly four
places: the provision bootstrap, the task-consent decision, and the two
step-up documents. Everything else was built by `buildTrustTask` and handed to
a channel that attached nothing, so it was refused with `proofRequired` before
a handler saw it.

Item 7 admits **no transport substitute**, which is why none of what we already
had counted: the REST bearer authenticates the connection, the TSP outer
signature authenticates the frame, and the DIDComm authcrypt authenticates the
sender of a message a mediator then forwards. None of them says the party named
in `issuer` vouched for this payload.

## The channel signs, not the caller

`signOutboundTask` is called by `RestChannel.post`, `TspChannel.packForVta` and
`DidcommVtaTransport.packEnvelope` — the one place each transport funnels
through on the way out. The ~116 sites that call `buildTrustTask` are
untouched, which is the point: signing at each of them is the same decision
taken 116 times, and forgetting once is a task that breaks the day someone
turns a check on. It is the shape `vta-sdk` took for the same problem
(`ClientIdentity`, signed in `dispatch_trust_task`).

A `SigningIdentity` is a **required** channel input rather than an optional
one, so the compiler refuses a channel that would send unsigned documents.
`loadHolder` already returns `signing` beside `identity`; the key lives in the
offscreen document's PRF cache, where task dispatch already runs, so no new
user gesture and no move off the background worker.

Signing is unconditional rather than keyed on the specification's
`isProofRequired`, for the reason vta-sdk gives: a proof on a task that merely
RECOMMENDs one is legal and strictly more attributable, and the alternative is
a 141-entry table that goes stale invisibly.

## Two things that fell out

`DidcommVtaTransport.exchange` and `buildOutbound` both built envelopes with no
`recipient`, so all four passkey-VM tasks were sending documents item 5b makes
malformed and item 8 cannot audience-bind. A signed document naming no audience
is replayable at another VTA, which is most of what signing was meant to buy.
Both now route through one `buildRequest`.

`signOutboundTask` refuses an envelope whose `issuer` is not the signer
(`e.client.identity`) rather than spending a round-trip discovering the
consumer's item-6 rejection.

## Layering

`trust-tasks` and `vta` were one layer, and same-layer imports are refused —
putting the signer on the channel's path needed `trust-tasks` to move below
`vta`. That is the fix the rule itself prescribes ("the shared part belongs one
layer down"), it costs nothing (`trust-tasks` imports only `didcomm` and
`siop`, and never referenced `vta`), and it tightens the check rather than
loosening it. No `KNOWN_EXCEPTIONS` entry was added.

## Deliberately not signed

The `/auth/` handshake (`vta/auth.ts`): that route is bespoke, authenticates by
the authcrypt sender, and never reaches the dispatch spine — vta-service reads
`msg.body["session_id"]` off the DIDComm envelope, which is the shape we send.
And `provision/integration`, which signs its own document with an
`authentication`-purpose proof in `provision/request.ts` and sends outside the
channels; routing it through one would overwrite that proof with an
`assertionMethod` one.

## Tests

`tests/vta.outbound-signing.mjs` runs the real verifier over the document as
the counterparty receives it — unpacked with real DIDComm and real TSP crypto
— rather than asserting a `proof` member exists, which a signature copied from
another document would satisfy. Confirmed it has teeth by removing the signer's
`delete docCopy.proof` and watching the re-signing case fail.

Also bumps `@openvtc/trust-tasks` to 0.16.3. It adds only
`consent/approve-request/0.1` — the prompt a VTA pushes to a designated
approver's phone, which this wallet does not implement — so nothing else here
moves.

title: chore(deps): trust-tasks 0.17.3, and retire the consent-prompt debt entry
body:
**Yes — and VTI was further behind than just the one crate.** Four of the five were two releases back:

| crate | was | now |
|---|---|---|
| `trust-tasks-rs` | 0.17.2 | **0.17.3** |
| `trust-tasks-capability-client` | 0.17.1 | **0.17.3** |
| `trust-tasks-didcomm` | 0.17.1 | **0.17.3** |
| `trust-tasks-https` | 0.17.1 | **0.17.2** |
| `trust-tasks-proof` | 0.17.1 | **0.17.2** |

**No manifest change.** Every requirement is already `"0.17"`, which admits all of these — the drift was purely a stale lockfile, the kind nothing reports until something asks.

### The guard fired, as designed

0.17.3 carries `consent/approve-request/0.1`, published upstream in [dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#331](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/331). That makes the `PRODUCED_UNPUBLISHED` entry from #1181 stale, and its shrink-only guard said so on the first run after `cargo update`:

```
these have a published spec now and must be removed from PRODUCED_UNPUBLISHED:
  https://trusttasks.org/spec/consent/approve-request/0.1
```

Publishing a spec cannot silently leave debt recorded claiming otherwise. Entry removed; the full cycle — add entry, publish spec, guard fails, remove entry — has now run end to end.

### A new obligation, and a test for it

Publishing the schema creates something that did not exist while there was none: **what we send must match what we published.**

Nothing on this side would catch a divergence. The prompt is *produced*, never served, so it never reaches the dispatcher's `validate_payload` — the party that validates it is the approver's device. A mismatch would therefore surface as a refused prompt on someone's phone, not a failing build. That is precisely the shape of both shipped payload defects this workspace has had (#895, #919): found by a person, from a rejected request in production.

So the wake test now validates the document it builds against the published schema. I confirmed it has teeth by adding a member the schema forbids and watching it fail, rather than trusting that it would.

Closes the last VTI-side item on #1177. `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets` → 0; full workspace suite passes.

title: feat(consent): specify consent/approve-request/0.1 with proof REQUIRED
body:
The prompt an agent's home service pushes to a designated approver, asking a human whether the agent may act on one conversation.

It was already being sent — by OpenVTC's VTA, over DIDComm to the approver's device — with no published schema on either side and no registry page a second implementation could work from. Found by a census in that repo ([OpenVTC#1177](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/issues/1177)).

### `proofRequirement: REQUIRED` is the substance

Not a formality. The document is **rendered to a person** and asks them to authorise an agent's access to a conversation. Without a proof the only thing vouching for it is the transport, so anything that can reach the approver's inbox can pose a question in the service's name — and the approver has no way to tell.

It is also the sole carrier of the `challenge` that the answering `consent/decision` must echo. An unauthenticated prompt therefore lets an attacker choose the value the approver will sign.

The consumer requirement is stated where it bites: **verify before rendering.** A prompt that fails verification is not a prompt, and rendering it anyway moves the authentication decision onto the one participant with no means to make it.

### Three payload decisions the prose argues rather than asserts

**`conversationRef` MUST be opaque.** A consent record naming raw platform addresses is a stored directory of who the subject talks to, readable by anyone who reaches the store. `displayHint` carries the recognisable name instead — bounded at 256 chars, and explicitly untrusted text a renderer must escape, since it's chosen by the requesting party.

**`kind` is not decoration.** Consenting to an agent reading a 1:1 exposes two parties; consenting on a group exposes everyone in it, most of whom are not being asked. An approver SHOULD be shown it.

**`firstMessageDigest` is a digest, not content.** The approver is deciding whether the agent may *read* the conversation; showing them the message in order to ask would disclose the very thing the decision gates.

### Shape

Fire-and-forget — no response document. The approver answers with a separate, separately-signed `consent/decision`, which is where the decision lives. `sideEffects: none` for the same reason: nothing is granted here.

`exposure.ingests: personal` while `discloses: metadata` — the asymmetry is deliberate and the rationale says why: the prompt puts a description of the subject's communications onto a device the requesting service does not control.

### Checks

`npm run build` clean — 350 specs validated, 66 shared schemas indexed, and it passes the freshness, free-text-bounds, error-code-casing and error-code-shadowing floors. Rust and TypeScript bindings regenerated in the same commit per CONTRIBUTING-SPECS; `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --all-features` and workspace clippy both clean. DCO-signed.

title: feat(vtc-service)!: enforce Trust Task Context Binding on presented credentials
body:
Closes #1065.

`taskContext` had zero occurrences in `vtc-service`. DTG Credentials marks it
REQUIRED on the VWC and defines Trust Task Context Binding as the mechanism that
keeps a credential from escaping the exchange that produced it. Security
Considerations 5 names what its absence permits — **context collapse**: a
credential that is genuinely signed, correctly typed, unrevoked and in date,
presented as evidence that *this* ceremony reached its terminal state when it was
issued during some other exchange entirely.

The ceremony pipeline was exposed to precisely that. It evaluates credentials as
facts and decides on them, and nothing in a fact said which exchange a credential
came from.

## What this does

Follows the division of labour `credentials::witness` (#1161) established — the
host settles what needs storage or keys, the policy branches on a settled state.

**Captured.** `VerifiedPresentation` gains `task_context`, read at verify time
from the credential's top level. It had to be captured *there* for the same
reason `credential_status` is: the DI and bbs paths keep only
`credentialSubject` in `claims`, so a `taskContext` read downstream would have
been unconditionally absent on those paths — a verifier structurally unable to
see the binding it is required to enforce.

**Enforced on receipt.** A VWC with no `taskContext` is refused, at both ingress
points: `credentials::ingress::classify_dtg` for JSON-LD arrivals (where the
catalog's own `TryFrom<DTGCommon>` puts the identical check) and the
credential-exchange present path for SD-JWT-VC / DI / bbs arrivals. Refused
rather than defaulted to the current thread — defaulting would manufacture the
binding being checked, and would award the strongest possible verdict to the
credential least entitled to it.

**Asserted in the evidence.** `Context.thread_id` names the exchange the ceremony
*is*; `Credential.task_context` names where each credential came from, as a
resolved `TaskContextBinding` (`sameExchange` / `foreignExchange` / `absent` /
`unthreaded`). A policy asserting an outcome can now require `sameExchange`.
Without the pair, "a credential from another exchange" is not expressible at all.

The end-to-end tests are the argument: the *same* well-formed, signed, in-date
witness admits or is rejected under one policy depending only on the exchange its
`taskContext` names.

## Decisions a reviewer should check

1. **A mismatch is reported, not refused.** A VWC's `taskContext` names the
   exchange the *witnessing* happened in — never the join exchange it is later
   presented in — so rejecting on mismatch would refuse every honest witness. The
   specification draws the same line: a verifier "MUST NOT interpret a
   `taskContext`-bearing credential as proof that the associated trust task
   completed unless the matching trust task outcome evidence is also present and
   verified". So absence (a malformed VWC) is an error; a foreign exchange is a
   fact the policy weighs.
2. **No shipped policy was tightened.** For the reason above: the default join
   and personhood policies read a VWC as background evidence of personhood, not
   as terminal-state evidence, and requiring `sameExchange` there would deny every
   legitimate witness.
3. **Thread ids are compared verbatim.** DTG Credentials specifies no
   canonicalization for `taskContext`, so there is no sanctioned way to decide
   that `urn:uuid:x` and `x` are one thread. Guessing fails open (a foreign
   credential accepted as local); comparing verbatim fails the other way. Pinned
   by a test so a later normalization has to be a deliberate change.
4. **Facts keys stay `snake_case`.** `context.thread_id` and
   `task_context.thread_id` follow the Rego facts contract (`facts.rs` documents
   `snake_case` keys as load-bearing — compiled policies read the literals), and
   match `witness_binding.relationship_id` beside them. The camelCase in this
   feature is `taskContext`, read *off the credential*, where the DTG spec
   dictates it.
5. **`presentation_from_verified_set` became fallible**, and refuses the whole
   presentation rather than dropping the offending credential — silently
   discarding one turns a malformed submission into a decision taken on less
   evidence than the holder believes it supplied.

## Deliberately not included

**Issuance (the issue's part 1).** Nothing in this workspace mints a VWC —
`dtg_credentials::DTGCredential::new_vwc` has no caller anywhere in VTI — so there
is no issuance flow to carry `taskContext` through, and adding one would be
inventing a feature rather than closing this gap. The catalog constructor already
takes `task_context: String` as a required parameter, so the first issuance path
cannot omit it. `taskContext` is OPTIONAL on every other DTG type, so it was not
added to the VMC / VEC / VIC the VTC does mint — that would change the wire shape
of every credential this service issues for no requirement, and the spec's own
note warns against reading such a credential as proof a task completed.

## Verification

- `cargo fmt --all`
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets` — 0 warnings
- `cargo test -p vtc-service --all-features` — pass
- `cargo test -p vta-service --all-features` — pass (rebased onto #1176)

Rebased on current `main` (`42cb978f`). The `semver report` check going red is
expected — no version was edited.

title: fix(inbound): validate the last two payloads still read by hand
body:
`parseTaskConsentRequest` was validated against its published schema in #128;
these are the two paths that were left.

**`parseRemovalNotice`** transcribed the `code` and `disposition` enums as
literals. That is correct only until the registry adds a value, at which point a
legitimate notice is dropped in silence and a member is not told they were
removed from a community. The schema is the copy that cannot fall behind
itself, and it enforces two things the hand version had no way to:
`additionalProperties: false`, and the bound on `reason` — the prose this
surface renders as the member's only account of why.

**The `decision/0.1#response` branch of `parseTaskConsentOutcome`** read
`status` as any string where the schema says `granted | pending | denied`, and
let a REQUIRED `payloadDigest` be silently absent. This is *not* the fail-open
the request path had — nothing branches on `status`, it is logged — so it is
validated for a narrower reason: "the executor said granted" should stay a claim
worth trusting when something eventually does branch on it.

**The `trust-task-error` branch is deliberately left unvalidated**, and says so.
It carries the executor refusing an approval a human already gave, and the one
thing that must not happen is failing to tell them. Rejecting a malformed error
document would drop that notification because the *refusal* was malformed —
strictly worse than reporting one whose members are read defensively, as they
are, member by member.

Validating found the same fixture drift a third time: `payloadDigest: "abc123"`
in five places, where the schema requires a `DigestMultibase`. The hand-read
accepted it every time. That is now three separate test files that had been
carrying non-conforming digests since the multibase cutover, each found by
turning a schema on rather than by anybody reading them.

Also documents the `tsc -b` trap that cost two wrong turns during the 0.5.0
release: `rm -rf packages/core/dist` leaves the `.tsbuildinfo`, so the next
build believes the output is current, prints nothing, exits 0 and emits no
files. Every dependent workspace then fails with "cannot find module", which
reads like a broken package. It is the nastier sibling of the stale-`dist` note
already in CLAUDE.md — there the build tells you something is wrong; here it
reports success.

title: test(vta): census the URIs this service produces, not just the ones it serves (#1181)
body:
test(vta): census the URIs this service produces, not just the ones it serves (#1181)

Three harnesses already police the task surface and a document can slip
between all three. `UNSPECCED_DISPATCHED_URIS` is per-URI and shrink-only
but tracks what the dispatcher **serves**. `producer_payload_conformance`
drives client methods, so it only sees payloads reached through a
`VtaClient` method. The VTC's manifest census scans source, but its prefix
is `https://trusttasks.org/openvtc/vtc/` — the VTC's private namespace — so
a public `spec/` URI never matches it wherever it runs.

`consent/approve-request/0.1` fell through all three, which is why it
shipped unsigned for as long as it did: **serving** an unspecced URI fails
the build, while **producing** one was invisible.

Every `spec/` literal under `vta-service/src` must now be published, served
(where the other harness owns the debt), or listed with a reason. Shrink-only
in both directions, matching the served-side list: a new entry fails rather
than being a line someone adds, and an entry whose spec has landed fails too.

It found two on the day it was written. `vta/attestation/{status,report}/1.0`
are REST-routed rather than dispatched, so the served-URI harness never saw
them — and `status` is unauthenticated and internet-reachable, the thing a
verifier checks before deciding to trust this VTA at all. Both recorded
against #1177.

Three literals are deliberately not counted, each stated rather than
silently skipped: `format!` templates carrying `{version}`, prefix constants
ending in `/`, and the `trust-task-error/*` family — which *is* in the
registry, but `schema_index` carries payload schemas for tasks, so
`schema_for` answers `None` and using that as the published-check would
report a published document as debt.

Negative fixtures are an explicit list, not a heuristic. Inferring "is this
inside a test module" from source text would be wrong occasionally and
silently, and this only works if a failure means something.

Both guards verified by mutation rather than assumed: renaming the produced
consent URI makes the census fail, and adding an already-published URI to
the tracked list makes the shrink guard fail.

Refs #1177.

title: fix(consent)!: sign the approve-request prompt sent to an approver's device (#1180)
body:
fix(consent)!: sign the approve-request prompt sent to an approver's device (#1180)

`consent/approve-request/0.1` was constructed as a bare `id` / `type` /
`issuedAt` / `payload` document and buffered to an approver's mediator for
delivery to their phone, where a human is asked to approve something. It
carried no proof, so nothing the device could check authenticated it.

This is the odd one out rather than a deliberate exception. The sibling
task-consent request in `consent_request.rs` already signs with this key and
cryptosuite, and the step-up prompt's mobile parser refuses to render
without a verified proof from an enrolled issuer
(`vta-mobile-core::task::parse_step_up_request` — "no valid proof from an
enrolled executor, no prompt"). Both end up in front of a person.

`issuer` and `recipient` come with the proof, not as decoration: SPEC §7.2
item 5b makes `recipient` REQUIRED and item 6 requires the in-band issuer to
match the transport identity. A proof over a document naming neither party
is replayable at a different approver, which is most of what the signature
was supposed to buy.

Fails closed. The wake path is best-effort and already warns on a failed
buffer, leaving the approver to mediator pickup; an unsignable prompt takes
the same route. "No prompt" is recoverable in a way "unverifiable prompt"
is not.

## Sequencing

This changes nothing about security on its own, because nothing verifies it
yet, and that is the reason to land it now rather than later: the fleet has
to be signing before devices can require a signature. Device-side
enforcement in `vta-mobile-core` follows, and must not ship first or it
breaks every VTA that has not deployed this.

Publishing the spec with `proof` REQUIRED is the third step, so the
requirement is normative rather than local convention. Tracked in #1177.

The test runs the real verifier over the document as sent rather than
asserting a `proof` member exists — a signature copied from another document
would satisfy the weaker check — and pins `issuer` and `recipient`.
Confirmed it has teeth by swapping the recipient DID and watching it fail.

Refs #1177.

title: feat(vtc): state artifact lifecycle precedence once, and apply it on read
body:
Closes #1079.

#1075 fixed an instance: an expired VRC became a permanent edge because
`routes/relationships.rs` read neither `validFrom` nor `validUntil`. It did not
fix the class. Nothing in the workspace established **precedence between a
cryptographically valid but stale artifact and a later lifecycle event**, and
the relationship graph had no vocabulary beyond "the row exists" and "the row
was deleted".

## The rule, stated once

`vtc-service/src/credentials/lifecycle.rs` is new and owns the vocabulary and
the precedence rule:

> A later recorded event takes precedence over the artifact's own earlier
> assertion, but only in the restrictive direction. An event can put an
> artifact out of force at any time; **no event can put an artifact into force
> that its own window excludes.**

Two clocks, kept separate:

- **validity time** — the window the issuer stated inside the artifact, fixed
  at issuance and covered by its signature (`ValidityWindow`).
- **transaction time** — what this service recorded about it afterwards
  (`LifecycleLog`, append-only and monotonic).

`resolve` combines them, and ignores events recorded *after* the instant being
asked about. That is what makes "was this in force last Tuesday" answerable at
all: without it, a suspension recorded today would retroactively make
yesterday's decision look wrong and the audit trail could not be reconciled
against the decisions it records.

**The asymmetry is the design.** Precedence exists so a community can end an
artifact's effect without waiting for its window and without a status list —
which is exactly why it matters here, since a VRC deliberately carries no
`credentialStatus` (D7). Running it the other way would let a recorded event
manufacture validity the issuer never signed for, a far worse failure than an
edge that lingers. So `Restored` returns an artifact to the governance of its
own window rather than extending it: restoring an edge that expired while
suspended succeeds and still reports `expired`.

**Restoration versus replacement is explicit.** `Restored` reverses a
suspension and nothing else. `Withdrawn` and `Superseded` are terminal — the
party relying on an artifact between a withdrawal and its reversal was entitled
to treat it as gone, and a log that can take a terminal state back cannot
answer the question it exists to answer. Effect is given back by issuing a
fresh artifact: a new signature, a new window, and a record that a *new*
assertion was made rather than an old one quietly resumed.

The module also states what a verifier elsewhere may conclude when current
state is deliberately undiscoverable (issue point 5): only that the artifact
was validly issued and is inside its window — never that it is in force, since
it cannot see whether a later event displaced it.

## Applied to relationships

- `Relationship` carries an append-only `lifecycle` log —
  `#[serde(default, skip_serializing_if = ...)]`, the same treatment `persona`
  got in #1067, so pre-existing rows decode and re-serialise unchanged.
- `Relationship::in_force_at` is the single resolution entry point. An
  unreadable window resolves to `Indeterminate` rather than defaulting to
  unbounded — rows written before #1075 entered the graph without their window
  ever being parsed, and treating an unreadable bound as "no bound stated" is
  the failure mode that makes the whole check ornamental.
- **`GET /v1/relationships/graph` now calls an edge `complete` only when an
  *in-force* VRC exists in both directions.** This is the direct fix for the
  symptom the issue names: a half-edge whose reciprocal had expired was
  indistinguishable from one that never arrived. Halves are still listed
  whatever their state — the credential was published, and hiding it would make
  a lapsed edge look like one that never existed.
- **`POST /v1/relationships/{id}/suspend` and `/restore`**, authorized by the
  same three routes revocation uses (issuer session DID, admin, or a `pop`
  proving control of a pairwise issuer), with distinct authorization `type`s so
  a suspend signature cannot be replayed to delete. That gate is now one
  function rather than a copy per verb — three copies of a three-branch
  authorization check is how the window check ended up implemented three ways
  and enforced on one path.
- **Supersession on republish.** Publishing a VRC to a counterparty the issuer
  already has an edge to records the displacement on the earlier row. An
  idempotent republish (same digest) returns early and displaces nothing.

`credentials::ingress` gains `validity_window`, sharing its reader with
`check_validity_window`, so admission and interpretation cannot disagree about
where a window's edges are. New audit variants `VrcSuspended` / `VrcRestored` /
`VrcSuperseded`; supersession is recorded under the *displaced* edge, not
folded into the publish entry for the credential that replaced it.

## Decisions a reviewer should check

**1. Automatic supersession on `(issuer, subject)`.** The judgement call in
this PR. DTG Credentials requires an R-DID to be unique per counterparty, so
the pair identifies the relationship and a second VRC for it is a new *version*
of one assertion rather than a second relationship. Before this both rows
accumulated and nothing said which one the issuer currently stood behind. If
the intended reading is that a member may hold several concurrent edges to one
counterparty (different endorsement types, say), this is wrong and supersession
should require the new credential to name the one it replaces — which DTG has
no field for today.

**2. `complete` changed meaning without the graph response saying why.**
`relationships/graph/0.2` pins the response with `additionalProperties: false`,
so a per-half `state` cannot be added here. An operator sees that a pair
stopped being complete but not which half lapsed and how. Fixing that needs a
`graph/0.3` upstream; the spec moves first.

**3. Same spec lag on the list route.** `Relationship` is both the stored row
and the item shape of `relationships/list/0.2`, whose schema predates
`lifecycle` — as it already predates `persona`. A listed edge with a lifecycle
event carries a member the published task does not describe. Recorded in the
field's doc comment rather than papered over by dropping it on the way out:
hiding the log from the one surface a member can read would leave them able to
be suspended and unable to see it.

**4. New routes carry no Trust-Task binding.** No canonical
`spec/vtc/relationships/{suspend,restore}` URI is published, and
`every_bound_canonical_task_exists_in_the_registry` requires a bound URI to
resolve in `schema_index`. Binding a URI that does not exist would trade a real
gate for a string, so these mount plain, the same exemption the `schemas`
routes carry, with a comment saying so.

## What this deliberately leaves

- **VPC, VMC and the recognition/VIC paths are untouched.** The types take a
  window and a log rather than a `Relationship`, so any of them can be brought
  under the same rule without a second precedence implementation appearing —
  but doing so is a change to each of those surfaces and belongs with them. The
  VIC and recognition paths in particular carry semantics the shared check does
  not (they *require* `validUntil`, and recognition clamps a minted session TTL
  to the earliest one), which is why #1075 left them alone and this does too.
- **`DELETE /v1/relationships/{id}` still deletes the row** rather than
  recording a `Withdrawn` tombstone. The vocabulary has the verb and the
  storage layer would take it; retaining a durable record that a pairwise edge
  once existed and was withdrawn is a privacy decision, not a refactor, and it
  is the same decision that removed `credentialStatus` from the VRC. Same
  reasoning for the VPC detach path the issue mentions.
- **Approval freshness after an authority change** (the last bullet of "what is
  missing") is not addressed. Re-evaluating an approval against a credential
  whose authority has since changed is `policy_gate`'s territory and needs the
  approval side to record what it relied on, which nothing does yet.

## Tests

`credentials::lifecycle` unit tests pin the rule directly: a later event beats
a still-valid artifact; no event puts one back inside a closed window; an event
does not apply before it was recorded; every terminal and transition boundary.
`routes::relationships` pins the graph read against expiry, suspension,
restoration, supersession and an unreadable window. `relationships::storage`
pins persistence, refusal-writes-nothing, and that supersession skips an
already-terminal row rather than failing an unrelated publish. Integration
tests exercise suspend/restore end to end through the HTTP surface, including
the 403/404/409 paths and the audit entries, plus supersession on the real
pairwise publish path.

title: Cross-artifact lifecycle precedence: suspension, supersession, restoration
body:
## Summary

#1075 fixed an instance: an expired VRC became a permanent edge because the
relationship route read neither `validFrom` nor `validUntil`. It did not fix the
class. Nothing in this workspace establishes **precedence between a
cryptographically valid but stale artifact and a later lifecycle event**, and
several credential types have no lifecycle vocabulary at all beyond "exists" and
"deleted".

Filing the general problem so the instance fix does not stand in for it.

## Why the instance was reachable

Two defensible decisions composed into an unreachable state:

1. The relationship graph is read **without re-checking dates**. Reasonable on
   its own — the edge was validated at ingress.
2. A VRC carries **no `credentialStatus`**, per planning-review D7. Also
   reasonable, and deliberately so: a status-list host learns which verifier
   checked which credential and when, which is the correlation the pairwise work
   exists to remove.

Neither is wrong. Together they leave `DELETE /v1/relationships/{id}` as the only
removal path, so a valid-forever artifact has no lifecycle at all.

**The deliberate absence of revocation is what makes precedence load-bearing.**
Where a credential type omits status for privacy reasons — which we think is
usually the right call — precedence and effective-time rules become the only
remaining lifecycle mechanism, not a refinement on top of revocation.

## What is missing

No shared vocabulary or precedence rule for:

- **suspension** — temporarily ineffective, not withdrawn
- **supersession** — a later artifact displacing an earlier one
- **restoration** — and its boundary against replacement or fresh grant
- **effective time and event precedence** across composed artifacts
- **transaction-time state discovery**, including what a verifier does when
  discovery is deliberately unavailable because the presentation must carry what
  it needs
- **approval freshness after an authority change** — we re-evaluate approver-set
  membership at execution (`policy_gate.rs`), but nothing re-evaluates an
  approval against a *credential* whose authority has since changed

## Where it already bites

- **VRC** — no status, no suspension; #1075 gated ingress only, and the VIC and
  recognition paths deliberately keep their own window semantics rather than
  sharing the gate. Three paths, three answers.
- **Relationship graph** — since #1073 an edge is complete or half-complete, but
  neither state has a notion of *suspended*. A half-edge whose reciprocal has
  expired is indistinguishable from one that never arrived.
- **VPC** (#1074) — a persona annotation has no lifecycle of its own. Detaching
  is the only reversal, and there is no record that a correlation once existed
  and was withdrawn.
- **VDC**, when it lands — this is where it gets expensive. A delegation that can
  be suspended and restored is the whole point of a bounded appointment, and the
  design note already commits us to freshness-by-re-issuance rather than live
  lookup, which puts the entire weight on precedence rules we have not written.

## Proposed shape

1. A common lifecycle vocabulary across credential types, rather than per-type
   ad-hoc handling.
2. Effective-time and precedence rules for composed artifacts — which state
   controls at decision time when two valid artifacts disagree.
3. One transaction-time evaluation gate that every ingress path calls, extending
   `credentials::ingress` where #1075 put the window check, with any deviation
   documented at the call site rather than implied.
4. Explicit restoration-versus-replacement semantics.
5. A statement of what a verifier may conclude when authoritative current state
   is deliberately undiscoverable.

## Provenance

The instance is ours (#1075, conformance-review finding F9). The generalisation
is external: it matches RAHP finding **F-003** in
`sankarshanmukhopadhyay/rahp-toolkit#66`, which arrived at the same residual from
a guardianship/fiduciary pressure test rather than from our code. Evidence from
our instance is posted there.

Note the numbering collision: RAHP's **F-003** and our conformance review's
**F3** are unrelated. This issue is the general form of our **F9**.

title: feat(vtc): state artifact lifecycle precedence once, and apply it on read (#1179)
body:
feat(vtc): state artifact lifecycle precedence once, and apply it on read (#1179)

Closes #1079.

#1075 fixed an instance: an expired VRC became a permanent edge because the
relationship route read neither `validFrom` nor `validUntil`. It did not fix
the class. Nothing in the workspace established precedence between a
cryptographically valid but stale artifact and a later lifecycle event, and
the relationship graph had no vocabulary beyond "the row exists" and "the row
was deleted".

## The rule, stated once

`vtc-service/src/credentials/lifecycle.rs` is new and owns the vocabulary and
the precedence rule:

> A later recorded event takes precedence over the artifact's own earlier
> assertion, but only in the restrictive direction. An event can put an
> artifact out of force at any time; no event can put an artifact into force
> that its own window excludes.

Two clocks, kept separate: validity time (the window the issuer signed) and
transaction time (what this service recorded afterwards). `resolve` combines
them, and it ignores events recorded after the instant being asked about — so
"was this in force last Tuesday" is answerable, and a suspension recorded
today does not retroactively make yesterday's decision look wrong.

The asymmetry is the design. Precedence exists so a community can end an
artifact's effect without waiting for its window and without a status list;
running it the other way would let a recorded event manufacture validity the
issuer never signed for. `Restored` therefore returns an artifact to its own
window rather than extending it: restoring an edge that expired while
suspended succeeds and still reports `expired`.

Restoration versus replacement is explicit. `Restored` reverses a suspension
and nothing else; `Withdrawn` and `Superseded` are terminal. The party relying
on an artifact between a withdrawal and its reversal was entitled to treat it
as gone, so effect is given back by issuing a fresh artifact — a new
signature, a new window, and a record that a new assertion was made.

## Applied to relationships

- `Relationship` carries an append-only `lifecycle` log, defaulted and skipped
  when empty, the same treatment `persona` got in #1067; pre-existing rows
  decode and re-serialise unchanged.
- `Relationship::in_force_at` is the single resolution entry point. An
  unreadable window resolves to `Indeterminate` rather than defaulting to
  unbounded — rows written before #1075 entered the graph without their window
  ever being parsed.
- `GET /v1/relationships/graph` now calls an edge `complete` only when an
  *in-force* VRC exists in both directions. This is the direct fix for the
  symptom the issue names: a half-edge whose reciprocal had expired was
  indistinguishable from one that never arrived. Halves are still listed
  whatever their state.
- `POST /v1/relationships/{id}/suspend` and `/restore`, authorized by the same
  three routes revocation uses (issuer session DID, admin, or a `pop` proving
  control of a pairwise issuer). That check is now one function rather than a
  copy per verb — three copies of a three-branch authorization gate is how the
  window check ended up implemented three ways and enforced on one path.
- Publishing a VRC to a counterparty the issuer already has an edge to records
  supersession on the earlier row. An R-DID is unique per counterparty, so the
  pair is the relationship and a second credential for it is a new version of
  one assertion. Idempotent republish displaces nothing.

`credentials::ingress` gains `validity_window`, sharing its reader with
`check_validity_window`, so admission and interpretation cannot disagree about
where a window's edges are.

New audit variants `VrcSuspended` / `VrcRestored` / `VrcSuperseded`.
Supersession is recorded under the displaced edge, not folded into the
publish entry for the credential that replaced it.

## What this deliberately does not do

VPC, VMC and the recognition paths are untouched; the types here take a window
and a log rather than a `Relationship`, so they extend without a second
precedence implementation appearing. `DELETE /v1/relationships/{id}` still
deletes the row rather than recording a tombstone — retaining a durable record
of a withdrawn pairwise edge is a privacy decision, not a refactor.

title: Trust Task Context Binding is not implemented
body:
## Summary

`taskContext` does not appear anywhere in `vtc-service` or `vta-sdk` — zero
occurrences. DTG Credentials marks it REQUIRED for the VWC and defines Trust
Task Context Binding as the mechanism preventing a credential from escaping the
exchange that produced it.

## Detail

From the specification:

- §Trust Task Context Binding: "For credential types where this specification
  marks `taskContext` as REQUIRED (currently only the VWC), issuers MUST
  include it."
- Security Considerations 5, **context collapse**: "A credential presented
  outside the trust task exchange in which it was issued may be misinterpreted
  as evidence of a completed ceremony. The requirements of Trust Task Context
  Binding exist to prevent this class of attack and must be enforced by
  verifiers."

This stack has a full ceremony engine (`ceremony/{facts,verify,evaluate}.rs`)
that evaluates credentials as facts and decides on them — and no binding
between a credential and the exchange it came from.

## Why it matters

The named attack is exactly the one the ceremony pipeline is exposed to: a
credential that is cryptographically valid, correctly typed, and issued during
some *other* exchange, presented as evidence that *this* ceremony reached its
terminal state.

## Suggested fix

1. Carry `taskContext.threadId` through issuance for the credential types the
   specification requires it on.
2. Require it on receipt where required, and reject its absence rather than
   defaulting.
3. Make ceremony evidence assert the thread it belongs to, so a credential from
   another exchange cannot satisfy a fact in this one.

Worth scoping against the planned DTG Core Trust Task Protocols specification —
some of the surface may be settled there first, and
trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec#11 tracks the normative dependency on that
unpublished model.

Conformance audit finding **F3**.

title: feat(vtc-service)!: enforce Trust Task Context Binding on presented credentials (#1178)
body:
feat(vtc-service)!: enforce Trust Task Context Binding on presented credentials (#1178)

`taskContext` had zero occurrences in `vtc-service`. DTG Credentials marks it
REQUIRED on the VWC and defines Trust Task Context Binding as the mechanism
that keeps a credential from escaping the exchange that produced it; Security
Considerations 5 names what its absence permits — **context collapse**, where a
credential that is genuinely signed, correctly typed, unrevoked and in date is
presented as evidence that *this* ceremony reached its terminal state, when it
was issued during some other exchange entirely.

The ceremony pipeline was exposed to exactly that: it evaluates credentials as
facts and decides on them, and nothing in a fact said which exchange a
credential came from.

Three parts, following the division of labour `credentials::witness` (#1161)
established — the host settles what needs storage or keys, the policy branches
on a settled state:

- **Captured.** `VerifiedPresentation` gains `task_context`, read at verify
  time from the credential's top level. It had to be captured there for the
  same reason `credential_status` is: the DI and bbs paths keep only
  `credentialSubject` in `claims`, so a `taskContext` read downstream would
  have been unconditionally absent on those paths — a verifier structurally
  unable to see the binding it is required to enforce.

- **Enforced on receipt.** A VWC with no `taskContext` is refused, at both
  ingress points: `credentials::ingress::classify_dtg` for JSON-LD arrivals
  (where the catalog's own `TryFrom` puts the same check) and the
  credential-exchange present path for SD-JWT-VC / DI / bbs arrivals. Refused
  rather than defaulted to the current thread — defaulting would manufacture
  the binding being checked, and would award the strongest verdict to the
  credential least entitled to it.

- **Asserted in the evidence.** `Context.thread_id` names the exchange the
  ceremony *is*; `Credential.task_context` names where each credential came
  from, as a resolved `TaskContextBinding`. A policy asserting an outcome can
  now require `sameExchange`; without the pair, "a credential from another
  exchange" is not expressible.

A mismatch is reported, not refused. A VWC's `taskContext` names the exchange
the *witnessing* happened in, which is never the join exchange it is later
presented in, so rejecting on mismatch would refuse every honest witness. The
specification's own note draws that line: a verifier must not read a
`taskContext`-bearing credential as proof the associated task completed without
the matching outcome evidence. Thread ids are compared verbatim; there is no
specified canonicalization, and inventing one would fail open.

Not included: issuance. Nothing in this workspace mints a VWC — `new_vwc` has
no caller — so there is no issuance flow to carry `taskContext` through. The
catalog constructor already takes it as a required parameter, so the first
issuance path cannot omit it.

Refs #1065
